title: Red Sox's Craig Breslow Responds to Ben Rice and Cam Schlittler Criticism
description: The Red Sox did what they had to do for the two Yankees' stars.
fullText:
Red Sox's Craig Breslow Responds to Ben Rice and Cam Schlittler Criticism originally appeared on NESN. 

The Boston Red Sox have been impacted by two guys from their backyard, so to say, who are now with the New York Yankees in Cam Schlittler and Ben Rice.

Arguably the best pitcher in all of Major League Baseball, Schlittler played his college days at Northeastern.

Rice, one of the better offensive players in baseball over the past six months, is a New England guy as well. Ultimately, both players would look great in a Red Sox uniform and do a lot for the organization, but there's more to it than the Red Sox missing out on two guys who happened to grow up close to Fenway Park.

At the end of the day, the Red Sox and other teams in Major League Baseball didn't do what was needed to land both of them, and as a result, they're worse off.

The Yankees are the one team out of 29 others that did the right thing in this regard, but similar to every other team in baseball, New York has certainly missed on a lot of other players as well.

According to the latest report, the Red Sox scouted Rice and Schlittler during the draft process, but Craig Breslow responded on Monday morning in a perfect way, perhaps quieting some of the noise from frustrated fans.

"Ray Fagnant, who scouts New England for the Red Sox, recommended both players, but the team passed," the Boston Globe reported.

"I can't speak specifically about Schlittler or Rice. I wasn't here during their drafts. I think there are probably 28 other teams who are saying the exact same thing and what is most important is that we're taking steps to understand how do players like slip through the draft, slip past us, and make sure that when the next player with that ability, is in our backyard, we're taking every opportunity to make sure that they end up in a Red Sox uniform," Breslow said.

While the idea of having Schlittler and Rice in Boston is the right one, it's important to look at context here.

Neither of these guys were marquee prospects, big-time high school recruits, or even great players at every stage of their college careers.

The Red Sox weren't working with some Buster Posey, Stephen Strasburg, or Bryce Harper-caliber player in their backyard. If they were, another team would have selected them before them anyway.

It's easy to look back on what could have been, but truthfully, the same can be said for every team in Major League Baseball, especially the Yankees, who haven't made all the right decisions in their scouting department as well.

title: Four observations as Yankees now face elimination with ALDS Game 2 loss
description: The Yankees are one loss from elimination. Four key observations and takeaways from their ALDS Game 2 loss to the Rays.
fullText:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. - This was the Rays' way, on full display in a pivotal Game 2.

Put the ball in play, use speed and daring on the bases and force the defense - in this case a skittish group of Yankees infielders - to make plays, or mistakes.

Cam Schlittler wasn't at his best Monday night, but the Yankees threatened a franchise postseason record for errors in one game at Tropicana Field, where the Rays own a huge house advantage.

Under the dome and on the spongy artificial surface, the Yankees' 5-2 loss pushed them to the brink elimination as this best-of-five AL Division Series shifts to the Bronx on Wednesday night.

Here are our takeaways from a lost Game 2:

This is where it all unraveled, with a four-run fifth inning that broke open a 1-1 game.

Jonathan Aranda (single) and Junior Caminero (double) opened at second and third. From there, two misplays by rookie shortstop George Lombard Jr. led to two runs.

Schlittler was gone after 76 stressful pitches (7 hits, 1 walk, just 2 strikeouts), leading to Richie Palacios' sharp, two-run single off a full-count pitch by Brent Headrick.

Just before that two-out hit made it 5-1, Lombard - with a runner crossing in front of him as he fielded Jonny DeLuca's grounder - rushed a wide throw to first for an error.

The first two runs off Schlittler were the product of soft contact, but highlighted the Rays' ability to pressure a defense with their speed and ability to put the ball in play - even against a pitcher with three different fastballs at high octane who'll be a shoe-in Cy Young Award winner next month.

Both came with the Yanks' infield in.

Liam Hicks' soft bouncer toward second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. took away his play at the plate, settling for the out at first.

Next up, Chandler Simpson, possibly the fastest runner in game, sent a weak grounder to Lombard, who whiffed on a rushed backhanded attempt, looking for a play at the plate.

Originally scored an error, it went as an infield hit and the Rays had a 3-1 lead.

And it could've been even worse.

Tampa Bay led 1-0 after the first, an inning where the Yanks' committed three errors - including a throwing error by second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. that scored the unearned run.

Chisholm's second errant toss cost the Yanks a synch inning-ending double play, but Schlittler picked up his teammates in that 19-pitch frame.

It started with a leadoff error by third baseman Ryan McMahon on Yandy Diaz's grounder and included a would-be third strike erased by Austin Wells' catcher's interference on Liam Hicks.

The Yanks' inability to take care of the ball has been a fundamental issue at times, and it has cost them in postseason, most notably in the decisive World Series Game 5 vs. the Dodgers.

Chisholm's error was a reckless play; he had no shot at doubling up Caminero, who was well across first base as the second baseman's off-balance throw went wild.

Ben Rice's two-homer night gave him four in four postseason games this year.

Leading off the fourth inning against Peralta, the lefty-hitting Rice's game-tying solo home was the Yanks first hit Monday, after being one-hit in Game 1 by Drew Rasmussen and Bryan Baker.

Rice's love affair with the Trop continued with a solo shot in the eighth off lefty Ian Seymour, making Rice a .448 hitter (13-for-29) this year - including postseason - under St. Pete's outdated dome, with seven home runs and 12 RBI.

Of course, we were bound to have some catwalk chaos here too, when Spencer Jones' towering fly to start the second inning struck the B-ring (in play).

But right fielder Victor Mesa Jr. made the catch - which otherwise would've likely been a fly out to center.

Before the game, Yanks manager Aaron Boone said he though about some alteration to his lineup.

But he ultimately felt convicted in running back the same order that was no-hit by Drew Rasmussen into the eighth inning of Game 1.

Once change he could've made was for McMahon, who entered 1-for-14 vs. starter Freddy Peralta, who lasted 4.2 innings.

Yet to see a 2026 postseason at-bat entering Monday, Jose Caballero (0-for-2 career vs. Peralta) was one possible choice.

Anthony Volpe (2-for-4, double, HR career vs. Peralta) was another, but that small sample size, plus Boone's reluctance to play him at third base at the Trop was a factor.

McMahon (0-for-1) did draw a full-count walk that ended Peralta's night in the fifth inning.

title: Ben Rice hits two home runs in Yankees' Game 2 ALDS loss to Rays

title: Rays beat Yankees 5-2 to take 2-0 ALDS lead
description: (AP) — Richie Palacios hit a two-run single in a four-run fifth inning and the Tampa Bay Rays took advantage of New York’s sloppy defense, beating Cam Schlittler and the Yankees 5-2 on Monday night to take a 2-0 lead in their AL Division Series.The Rays are one victory from reaching the American League Championship Series.
fullText:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. (AP) — Richie Palacios hit a two-run single in a four-run fifth inning and the Tampa Bay Rays took advantage of New York's sloppy defense, beating Cam Schlittler and the Yankees 5-2 on Monday night to take a 2-0 lead in their AL Division Series.

The Rays are one victory from reaching the American League Championship Series. Game 3 in the best-of-five playoff is Wednesday night at Yankee Stadium.

Ben Rice hit a pair of homers for the Yankees, who are on the verge of elimination — which would extend their World Series drought to 17 seasons. They were dominated by Drew Rasmussen in the series opener and have scored just two runs in two games with three-time AL MVP Aaron Judge out of the lineup due to a calf injury.

The small-ball Rays chased Schlittler, the likely AL Cy Young Award winner, in the fifth aided by New York's defensive miscues.

Jonathan Aranda lined a single to start the inning and Junior Caminero ripped a double to right-center. With the infield drawn-in except second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr., who was standing several feet further back on the dirt, Liam Hicks hit a bouncer to second that scored Aranda for a 2-1 lead. Chisholm's only play was at first because he wasn't all the way in like the rest of the infielders.

Chandler Simpson then hit a grounder that shortstop George Lombard Jr. booted, scoring Caminero to make it 3-1. It was initially ruled a hit and then changed to an error and eventually a fielder's choice. Brent Headrick replaced Schlittler and struck out Victor Mesa Jr. After Simpson stole second, Jonny DeLuca reached on a grounder when Lombard's throw to first was wide for New York's fourth error.

Palacios followed with a hard single to center that increased Tampa Bay's lead to 5-1.

That was plenty of support for one of the best bullpens in the majors.

Freddy Peralta allowed one run and three hits in 4 2/3 innings, Cam Booser pitched out of a bases-loaded jam in the fifth and Ian Seymour gave up one run on Rice's solo shot in three innings. Bryan Baker finished with a perfect ninth for his second save in two games.

Schlittler, who was 14-6 with a 1.95 ERA and dominated Boston in the opener of the wild-card round, lasted 4 1/3 innings. He allowed four runs — two earned — and six hits. Schlittler only fanned two.

CLEVELAND (AP) — Braden Montgomery lined a two-run double down the right-field line, Sean Burke allowed one hit in 5 1/3 innings of splendid relief and Chicago beat Cleveland to take a 2-0 lead in their AL Division Series.

The surprising White Sox improved to 4-0 in these playoffs — all on the road — and are one win from advancing to the American League Championship Series for the first time since winning the World Series in 2005. Chicago became the first team to reach the postseason after three straight 100-loss seasons, including a post-1900 record 121 defeats in 2024.

Jo Adell hit an RBI triple in the eighth and Chase DeLauter had two hits for the Guardians.

Starting pitcher Gavin Williams struck out 11, tied for second-most in a Cleveland postseason game. But the offense failed to produce for the second straight game.

Grant Taylor worked 1 1/3 innings and allowed one hit as he got his second straight save.

The best-of-five series shifts to Chicago for Game 3 on Wednesday.

title: Disastrous defense sinks Yankees in ALDS Game 2 loss to Rays
description: For the second time in three years, the Yankees had a disastrous defensive game in the postseason and it cost them again, this time in a 5-2 loss to the Rays Monday night in Game 2 of the AL Division Series.
fullText:
For the second time in three years, the Yankees had a disastrous defensive game in the postseason and it cost them again, this time in a 5-2 loss to the Rays Monday night in Game 2 of the AL Division Series.

The Yanks made four errors in the loss, leading to three unearned runs, and they now teeter on the brink of elimination, down two games to none in the best-of-five series. Game 3 is set for Wednesday night at Yankee Stadium.

Two years ago, the Yankee defense collapsed in Game 5 of the World Series against the Dodgers and they were eliminated. But even that game only featured three Yankee errors – in the box score, anyway.

Monday's debacle was only the fifth time the Yankees have made four errors in a single postseason game. The last time was in the 2019 ALCS against the Astros.

The Yankees have scored only twice so far in the series, on two solo home runs by Ben Rice Monday night. No Aaron Judge, who is out with a calf injury, certainly doesn't help.

-- Yankee starter Cam Schlittler was not nearly as brilliant as he's been in his previous postseason outings. He lasted just 4.1 innings and allowed seven hits and four runs (only two earned). He struck out just two and didn't have a strikeout until the fourth inning and got only seven swings-and-misses. He also walked one. His career postseason ERA rose from 0.87 to 1.44.

-- The Yankees defensive implosion started in the very first inning and set a dubious club record for errors in a single postseason frame – three. The Yankees had never had three errors in one October inning and this is the 61st postseason appearance in the Yankees' existence. The Yanks last committed three errors in an inning in any game on Aug. 21, 2025 against the Red Sox. The last time it happened in any postseason game was Game 5 of the 2015 ALDS when the Rangers did it in a loss to the Blue Jays.

-- Ryan McMahon, who has a fine defensive reputation, though he has not had his best season with the glove, made the first miscue when the leadoff hitter, Yandy Díaz, hit a topspin bouncer to him that McMahon muffed. Jonathan Aranda followed with a single and then Junior Caminero hit what could've been a double-play grounder to short. George Lombard Jr. made a not-that-graceful flip to the bag and Jazz Chisholm Jr. grabbed it and threw wildly to first. Díaz scored and Caminero went to second.

Then it seemed like Schlittler had Hicks struck out, but, upon replay review, Austin Wells was called for catcher's interference – his mitt was clearly in the path of Hicks' bat. That was the third error of the inning. They nearly had a fourth – Chisholm fielded Simpson's grounder but threw high to second base, pulling Lombard off the bag. But Lombard got back in time for a force out. Schlittler got a grounder from Victor Mesa to mercifully end the inning. The Yankees only allowed one run, but all the gaffes forced Schlittler to endure some tense moments and extra pitches.

-- The Rays scored four runs in the fifth inning and knocked out Schlittler. They got some weak contact and used their speed to exploit it. Poor Yankee defense helped, too. Aranda started the inning with a single and Caminero followed with a ringing double. With the infield mostly in – Chisholm was further back than the rest of the infielders – Liam Hicks hit a grounder that was slow enough to allow Aranda to score.

Chandler Simpson later hit a soft grounder to short that Lombard couldn't backhand and another run scored. The scoring on that play was changed several times, but it was ultimately scored an infield single. But Lombard then made a throwing error to further prolong the inning and Richie Palacios added a single after an eight-pitch bout with reliever Brent Headrick that scored two more runs.

-- The Yanks went nine up, nine down the first time through their batting order as Rays starter Freddy Peralta looked sharp. But Rice tied the score at 1 with a 372-foot drive over the right-field fence. Rice connected on the fourth of four consecutive changeups from Peralta. Rice also homered in the eighth inning, giving him four home runs in four games this postseason.

-- In the fifth, the Yanks had a big chance with two outs, but could not cash in. Wells lashed a double into the right-field corner that looked a lot like the ball he hit in Game 1 and got thrown out trying to stretch into a triple. He wisely stopped at second this time. McMahon then worked a walk in a tough, seven-pitch at-bat. He was the last batter that Peralta faced. He came out with Rice coming up to the plate.

Rice worked another walk against southpaw Cam Booser, which brought up Cody Bellinger, who was 11th in MLB with a .340 average with runners in scoring position. Bellinger hit a deep fly ball to the warning track in center that held some hope, but it was caught.

-- Peralta, the former Met who got his pitching together in Tampa Bay, lasted 4.2 innings and allowed one run and three hits. He struck out three and walked one. The outing lowered his career postseason ERA from 4.32 to 4.03.

title: With Aaron Judge sidelined, Yankees' next generation takes over October
description: The Yankees are leaning on homegrown stars such as Ben Rice and Cam Schlittler in October as Aaron Judge remains out with a calf injury.
fullText:
Three summers ago, George Lombard Jr. was a high school shortstop in Miami. Now he's 21, playing shortstop in October and part of the reason the New York Yankees still believe they can get past the Tampa Bay Rays.

The Rays won Game 1 of the American League division series 1-0 on Saturday. Drew Rasmussen struck out 10 and held the Yankees to one hit, the fewest in their 447 postseason games. Teams that win Game 1 of a best-of-five series go on to win it about 73% of the time.

Monday night at Tropicana Field, the Yankees hand Game 2 to another one of their own picks. Cam Schlittler, a seventh-rounder out of Northeaster in 2022, led the AL with a 1.95 ERA. He went 14-6 and struck out 239 in 193⅔ innings. Only Spud Chandler in 1943 and Ron Guidry in 1978 posted a lower ERA for the Yankees as qualified starters.

Aaron Judge hasn't played since Sept. 16 because of a right calf strain. Without him, the Yankees have been winning with homegrown players. Ben Rice was a 12th-rounder out of Dartmouth in 2021. Spencer Jones went 25th overall out of Venderbilt in 2022, the same draft as Schlittler. Lombard went 26th overall out of Gulliver Prep in 2023.

Damon Oppenheimer's amateur scouting department drafted all four. Oppenheimer, the Yankees' vice president and director of amateur scouting, has run the club's draft since 2005. His department also took Judge 32nd overall out of Fresno State in 2013.

"I think it's been a very gratifying couple of weeks for our player development, and deservedly so," Yankees manager Aaron Boone said during a Zoom call Sunday.

Boone gave credit to Kevin Reese's player development staff for turning those draft picks into big leaguers, too.

"In a season where we've been beat up and banged up, we've had answers," Boone said.

Rice has been the loudest answer, and he made his presence known in 2025.

He went 4-for-5 in the wild-card opener against the Boston Red Sox with a double, a solo homer and an eighth-inning grand slam. His six RBI tied the franchise postseason record, and he became the first Yankees player with four hits and six RBIs in a playoff game. On Sunday, Boone joked that he almost pinch-hit Giancarlo Stanton for Rice right before the slam.

Matt Hyde, the Yankees' Northeast area scout, didn't find Rice at Dartmouth. He found him playing summer ball for the Worcester Bravehearts in the Futures League. The Yankees took Rice with the 363rd pick. This July he was an All-Star with 29 homers at the break and swung in the Home Run Derby.

Boston found that out first in the wild-card opener. Schlittler struck out 10 over 6 ⅓ scoreless innings to back Rice's performance. Both grew up in Massachusetts and played college ball in New England.

On Monday Schlittler goes against Freddy Peralta, the AL Pitcher of the Month for September. The Rays got Peralta from the Mets on Aug. 2. Boone said Tropicana Field really accentuates a good four-seam fastball, and that Tampa Bay has tweaked Peralta's mix so he uses his changeup "a good bit."

In Game 2 of the Yankees' wild-card series against the Red Sox, Jones became the first player in postseason history to score in an inning he started and ended the sixth with a strikeout. He reached on a dropped third strike, stole second, took third on a throwing error and scored on Lombard's single. New York put up six runs in the inning, which ended with Jones going down swinging.

Jones waited a long time for that. He hit 35 homers between Double-A and Triple-A in 2025, second most in the minors, and he wasn't called up this year until May. His first big-league homer on June 9 came off the bat at 112.2 miles per hour, the hardest-hit first homer by a Yankees player in the Statcast era. Yes, that includes Judge.

Lombard, the son of former big-leaguer George Lombard, debuted Aug. 4 and hit .237 with seven homers and 22 RBIs. In one inning against the Rays on Sept. 24, he jumped over the catcher to score on a pitch that got away, then came back and hit a go-ahead two-run homer into the second deck.

Boone said what impressed him most was how Lombard handled a bad week early on.

"He loves the game, which I think is always impressive," Boone said. "Like he loves the stuff that's not sexy, the behind the scenes, the grind the routine."

title: Chad Tracy’s controversial Game 1 move backfires as Red Sox fans react
description: Red Sox manager Chad Tracy is facing criticism after his fifth-inning pitching change backfired against the Yankees. Rookie Payton Tolle had allowed one run before Tracy replaced him with Erik Miller, who surrendered a solo homer to Ben Rice. Boston’s 9-0 loss intensified questions about the decision.
fullText:
The Boston Red Sox entered their postseason opener hoping rookie Payton Tolle could challenge the New York Yankees. Instead, one fifth-inning pitching change became a major talking point after Boston suffered a shutout defeat.

Manager Chad Tracy pulled Tolle with two outs and nobody on base, choosing left-handed reliever Erik Miller to face Yankees slugger Ben Rice. Three pitches later, Rice sent a fastball over the center-field wall.

The home run gave New York a two-run advantage, and Boston ultimately lost 9-0. Although the Yankees controlled much of the game, Tracy's decision immediately drew criticism from frustrated Red Sox fans.

Tolle started Game 1 of the American League Wild Card Series on Sept. 29 at Yankee Stadium. The 23-year-old rookie received the assignment after delivering encouraging performances during his first major league season.

Through four innings, Tolle had allowed one earned run on five hits while recording four strikeouts. He had also issued one walk, keeping Boston within striking distance despite facing New York's dangerous lineup.

The pivotal moment arrived in the bottom of the fifth. Tolle retired Paul Goldschmidt on one pitch for the second out, but Tracy decided to make a change with the left-handed Ben Rice approaching.

Tracy summoned Miller, another left-hander, to face Rice. The matchup appeared designed to neutralize the Yankees slugger, but the result quickly undermined the manager's decision.

Miller threw a 97-mph fastball that landed over the middle of the plate. Rice connected solidly, driving the pitch over the center-field fence for a solo home run that doubled New York's lead.

The sequence unfolded in only three pitches, turning an already scrutinized decision into an immediate talking point. Miller recorded just one out before Boston replaced him, leaving fans questioning the timing and reasoning behind the move.

Fun fact: Ted Williams remains the last MLB player to finish a season batting over .400, hitting .406 for Boston in 1941.

The home run triggered a wave of criticism on social media, with fans questioning why Tracy removed Tolle when the rookie had recorded two outs and faced nobody on base.

Some supporters argued that Tolle deserved an opportunity to finish the inning. Others focused on the decision to replace one left-handed pitcher with another, especially when Miller struggled during his final regular-season appearances.

One fan described the move as a bad decision, while another questioned why Boston would remove Tolle only to bring in a reliever who appeared less effective. The reaction reflected frustration with both timing and execution.

Tracy defended the change by pointing to the situation in the batting order. Rice had doubled earlier against Tolle, and the manager believed Miller offered a favorable opportunity to get the dangerous hitter out.

"Not necessarily just the pitch count, but you're trailing already, you're moving through the lineup for the third time," Tracy explained after the game, according to NBC Boston's report.

Tracy added that Rice had already hit a double against Tolle and that Miller presented a suitable matchup. The manager's explanation clarified his thinking, although the resulting home run intensified questions about the decision.

Tolle was not dominating every at-bat, but he had kept the Yankees' offense relatively contained. His five hits allowed and one earned run through 4⅔ innings gave Boston a chance to remain competitive.

The rookie had thrown 83 pitches when Tracy removed him. NBC Boston noted that Tolle exceeded that pitch count 20 times during the regular season, making the decision particularly noticeable to observers.

No one can know whether Tolle would have retired Rice or completed the inning successfully. However, his performance before the change gave critics a clear reason to question whether removing him was necessary at that moment.

While Boston's pitching decisions attracted attention, Yankees starter Cam Schlittler delivered the strongest performance of the night. He limited the Red Sox to two hits and one walk while striking out 10 batters over 6⅓ scoreless innings.

Schlittler's command and velocity repeatedly frustrated Boston's hitters, leaving the visitors unable to build meaningful offensive momentum. The Red Sox never scored, making it difficult to challenge New York even before the game's late innings.

The Yankees eventually won 9-0, scoring seven runs across the final two innings. That wider margin reflected Boston's broader struggles, meaning Tracy's fifth-inning decision was significant without being the only reason for the defeat.

Miller's appearance ended quickly after Rice's home run, forcing Boston to continue navigating its bullpen earlier than planned. The manager's choice also became more consequential as the game moved into its later innings.

The Red Sox struggled to contain New York after the fifth, and the Yankees extended their advantage with a powerful late offensive surge. Boston's pitching staff could not prevent the contest from becoming a lopsided defeat.

Although the game's final score magnified the scrutiny, the bullpen's overall performance and the offense's inability to score also mattered. The loss was a team result, even as Tracy's decision became its most debated managerial moment.

The 9-0 defeat left the Red Sox needing a response in Game 2 of the best-of-three Wild Card Series. Instead, New York won again and completed a two-game sweep.

Boston started veteran Sonny Gray in the second game, while the Yankees turned to left-hander Max Fried. Fried allowed 1 run over 6 innings, and New York pulled away for a 9-2 victory.

Tracy's handling of Tolle remained part of the postgame discussion, but Boston's broader problems also mattered. The Red Sox were outscored 18-2 across the series and were eliminated before reaching the Division Series.

The Red Sox lost 9-0 to the Yankees in Game 1 on Sept. 29, 2026.

Chad Tracy removed rookie starter Payton Tolle with two outs in the fifth inning.

Erik Miller replaced Tolle but gave up a solo homer to Ben Rice.

Fans criticized the timing of the pitching change and the lefty-on-lefty matchup.

Tracy said he wanted Miller to face Rice after the Yankees slugger had doubled earlier.

Boston then lost Game 2, 9-2, and was eliminated in a two-game Yankees sweep.

fullText:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — The Rays beat out the Yankees for first in the AL East and won more games than anyone in the league with one of the lowest payrolls playing an entertaining throwback style of aggressive baseball. They have three stars at the top of their lineup. They have a .300 hitter in the middle who can fly.

They bunt for hits, squeeze runners home and move runners better than anyone. Their rotation and bullpen are deep. Their record in one-run games was the best in the majors.

The Rays have the Yankees respect.

The Yankees also think they're the better team heading into a postseason showdown that seemed inevitable, a best-of-five Division Series between the two best teams in the league.

"At the end of the day, I think we played Tampa pretty well this year and I think we're in a good spot," Yankees ace Cam Schlittler said.

The Rays won the season series 7-6, but the Yankees feel they're peaking at the right time with their four aces finally all healthy at the same time.

They'll all be unleashed on the Rays. Gerrit Cole will start Saturday night's Game 1 at Tropicana Field, Schlittler will go Game 2, then the Yankees will go to their lefties when the series moves to New York with Carlos Rodon probably starting Game 3 and Max Fried pitching Game 4 if there's no sweep.

The Yankees' Division Series roster will be deeper than the 26-man squad that just swept the Red Sox in a Wild Card Series with 9-0 and 9-2 romps. Ryan Weathers is off the IL and available out of the bullpen, but Aaron Judge still isn't return to return from his Grade 2 calf strain.

The Yankees' one change from their their Wild Card Series roster was adding Weathers for an 11th pitcher and dropping infielder/outfielder Amed Rosario.

Second baseman Jazz Chisholm guaranteed the Yankees will win the series and Schlittler doubled down with "why would I disagree?"

The captain is also confident, regardless of his status.

"The Rays, they've got everything," Judge said. "It's a tough opponent. We're up in the task. We saw them all year. We had our battles, and we're just happy for the opportunity."

title: Yankees’ Gerrit Cole Ties CC Sabathia in MLB History
description: The New York Yankees made the call that folks weren’t sure they would make. Gerrit Cole is going to start Game 1 of the ALDS on Saturday against the Tampa Bay Rays. Despite struggles late in the season, Cole will get the ball for the game in Tropicana Field that could be crucial for the […] The post Yankees’ Gerrit Cole Ties CC Sabathia in MLB History appeared first on HEAVY.
fullText:
The New York Yankees made the call that folks weren't sure they would make.

Gerrit Cole is going to start Game 1 of the ALDS on Saturday against the Tampa Bay Rays.

Despite struggles late in the season, Cole will get the ball for the game in Tropicana Field that could be crucial for the Yankees to win in what is just a best-of-five series.

The Cole Train comes to Tampa for ALDS Game 1 🚂#RepBX pic.twitter.com/uTSBdY0ba3

— New York Yankees (@Yankees) October 2, 2026

Whether or not the Yankees should be starting Cole will only reveal itself on Saturday.

For now, there is a cool bit of history.

Cole has a long history of starting Game 1 in postseason series.

This will be his ninth Game 1 start (if you also include the single-game Wild Card Series that used to exist).

That's tied for fifth-most all-time, according to MLB Network's Sarah Langs.

Tied with Cole with nine of these starts? CC Sabathia.

In fourth place on the all-time Game 1 starts list is Greg Maddux, who had 11.

There's a tie for second place: Both Clayton Kershaw and Jon Lester started 12 of these games.

And alone in first place, potentially for a long time: Justin Verlander, with 14.

This will be the 9th time Gerrit Cole starts Game 1 of a postseason series (including singular Wild Card Game), tying CC Sabathia for 5th-most all time, behind:

Justin Verlander: 14
 Jon Lester: 12
 Clayton Kershaw: 12
 Greg Maddux: 11 https://t.co/NgopsVMhCQ

— Sarah Langs (@SlangsOnSports) October 2, 2026

Cole finished the 2026 regular season with a 3.61 ERA. That's his worst mark since 2017.

To be fair, it's still a really quality number, but Cole did prove a bit homer-prone late in the year. He also had his lowest strikeout rate (9.3 per nine innings) since that 2017 season, as well.

Cole has been a great playoff pitcher in his career. He has a 2.77 ERA in the postseason.

In the Yankees' 2024 playoff run to the World Series, he had a 2.17 ERA in five games.

Cole's most recent Game 1 start was in Game 1 of the 2024 World Series. He allowed just one run in six innings.

Cole has once faced the Rays in an ALDS Game 1, as well. That was in 2020. He went 6.0 innings and allowed three runs, including two home runs — Randy Arozarena with the first one, and Ji-man Choi with the second.

That game clearly has no real bearing on what happens on Saturday. The Rays beat the Yankees for the AL East title. Now, the Yanks will try and avenge that by potentially winning the ALDS. Cole will have to set the tone on the mound.

title: Another down-to-the-wire Yankees' decision on Aaron Judge's playoff status
description: Yankees captain Aaron Judge has been hitting against live pitching leading up to Saturday's AL Division Series opener. He has been on the injured list since Sept. 17, due to a right calf strain.
fullText:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. – With their spring training and minor league headquarters located across Tampa Bay, there's an at-home element for the Yankees here, too.

So, Aaron Judge made use of Steinbrenner Field in Tampa before participating in Friday's team workout at Tropicana Field.

Judge also hit against live pitching Thursday at Yankee Stadium, in hopes of being added to the AL Division Series roster against the AL East champion Rays.

"We'll see,'' manager Aaron Boone said Friday of Judge's status for best-of-five series, beginning Saturday night.

These Yankees are either facing another playoff round without Judge, or with a limited Judge, due to a moderate right calf strain suffered in a Sept. 16 game.

And they've already made an offensive impression, outscoring the Red Sox, 18-2, in a two-game sweep of the AL Wild Card Series at the Stadium.

Neither Judge nor Giancarlo Stanton – available on the bench as a pinch-hitter – took a swing against the Sox, but the Rays represent their greatest challenge toward claiming a second AL pennant in three years.

The captain also hadn't run the bases since his injury (through Thursday), but "they replicate things in other ways,'' said Boone. "The trainers will obviously play a big part in this.''

Judge might not be an option as a right fielder until next Wednesday, at the extreme minimum, when the series shifts to the Bronx.

The artificial surface at the Trop "plays into it a little bit, just as far as him in the field, potentially'' Boone said of the Judge decision.

"It's more (about) is he going to be available at some point in this series, potentially, as a player? That's what we're kind of weighing and then seeing where he's at now…having taken live BP.

"We'll see how (Friday) goes.''

Boone wasn't yet sure if the Yanks would be taking 10, 11 or 12 pitchers into the ALDS, which impacts the available players off his bench.

It's difficult to imagine both Stanton and Judge on the ALDS roster, in limited capacity. Of Stanton's ALDS status, Boone would only say: "We haven't decided that yet.''

Stanton made that cut for the Wild Card Series, activated for the first time since late April, due to a calf strain (and then two additional calf strains).

"To see velocity and try to visualize yourself out there,'' are Stanton's keys to Judge ramping up to playoff-level pitching, following a layoff.

Judge only had 24 September plate appearances in seven games, after missing 84 team games due to a fractured first right rib.

Personally, Stanton said it's "always good'' to get at-bats, but "I preferred to get two wins and be here now,'' on the eve of an ALDS.

"I'm just trying to win a championship now,'' Stanton said of that elusive prize in his 17th MLB season. "That's what's most important.''

Before the Wild Card Series, Judge, 34, brought up the "very short window'' to achieve his championship aim.

The captain also mentioned earlier how "this team has picked up the slack'' in his absence, and that was before the Wild Card sweep.

Boone said he expected that Ryan Weathers would be available, but no decision was made yet on the lefty's addition to the ALDS roster.

Weathers hasn't pitched in a big-league game since late August, due to a left flexor strain.

"I feel super healthy to be on (the roster),'' said Weathers, who a bullpen session Wednesday.

Weathers threw his second live BP to a group that included Stanton, Jose Caballero and Trent Grisham on Monday at the Stadium.

"I felt a lot sharper in the second one. Better location,'' said Weathers, whose challenge was facing "three of the most passive hitters in baseball'' with power.

If Weathers is added, lefty Ryan Yarbrough's roster spot could be in jeopardy.

fullText:
Red Sox star Willson Contreras speaks up on 'data' and 'computers after series loss to Yankees appeared first on ClutchPoints. 

As the Boston Red Sox's 2026 season ended with a two-game sweep by the New York Yankees in the American League Wild Card Series, veteran catcher Willson Contreras made his frustration with the organization's data-driven approach clear after Wednesday's loss.

Contreras had momentarily given Boston a glimmer of hope in the sixth inning when he launched a Statcast-projected 387-foot solo home run to right-center with two outs. The blast ended a 26-inning postseason scoring drought for the Red Sox dating back to Game 2 of last year's Wild Card Series, also against the Yankees. However, New York answered with six runs in the bottom of the inning, turning the game into a 9-2 defeat.

Boston was outscored 18-2 across the two games and was eliminated before getting a chance to play in October. The loss also extended the Red Sox's streak to five consecutive seasons without postseason baseball at Fenway Park.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

After the game, Contreras was asked about manager Chad Tracy's decision to remove starter Sonny Gray in the fifth inning. Gray had allowed six hits across 4 2/3 innings and surrendered only one run, a solo homer by Luis García Jr. He left after reaching 70 pitches with runners on the corners and two outs.

Tracy replaced Gray with left-handed reliever Erik Miller to face Cody Bellinger. Miller surrendered a run-scoring single to Bellinger before allowing another single to García. Gray had recorded a .180/.235/.280 slash line against hitters during their third time facing him this season, while Bellinger had been better against left-handed pitching than right-handed pitching. Contreras responded to the question about Gray by pretending to zip his mouth closed.

He was more direct when discussing Boston's broader reliance on data and technology.

"It's not enough when you have talent, or you have data, or you have computers telling you what to do, because this is baseball," said Contreras. "The data is here to help us but at the end of the day, you're going to need experience and veteran guys to win games. There's a lot of stuff that I would like to say, but I'll state it like that."

Willson Contreras: "It's not enough when you have talent, or you have data, or you have computers telling you what to do, because this is baseball. The data is here to help us, but at the end of the day, you need experience and veteran guys to win games. There's a lot of stuff I… pic.twitter.com/MS7u5yy96y

— Foul Territory (@FoulTerritoryTV) October 1, 2026

The comments came after the Red Sox's disappointing postseason exit and a regular season that featured major swings in performance. Boston fell into a 32-46 hole before going 32-5 from June 25 through August 7, including a franchise-tying 15-game winning streak.

The team then slumped during the final month amid injuries and offensive problems, which carried into the postseason. The Red Sox's bullpen also labored through a second consecutive difficult night against New York, while Garrett Crochet's return from shoulder and lat issues lasted less than an inning. Making his first appearance since April 25, Crochet failed to record an out and was charged with four runs.

Contreras' comments only added to the fallout from an elimination that exposed disagreements over Boston's decision-making and approach under chief baseball officer Craig Breslow.

title: Hand injury keeps Red Sox’ Roman Anthony out of lineup for Game 2 vs Yankees — and the rest of the Wild Card series
description: Losing 9-0 against your blood rivals to open off the postseason is bad enough. fullText:
Losing 9-0 against your blood rivals to open off the postseason is bad enough. But the pain of last night was brought to another level by losing 9-0 while your leadoff hitter and the face of the franchise mysteriously leaves the game after two awkward strikeouts.

As we discussed last night, Roman Anthony appeared to re-aggravate his bad right hand in the final game of the season against the Rays. And as OTM's Matt Gross points out, footage from last night shows that he had his hand heavily taped up prior to the game:

You can see in this picture from before last night's game that Roman Anthony's right hand was pretty heavily taped up leading into it. Whatever happened in Tampa was much worse than they initially let on. In hindsight, Anthony likely doesn't even start if it's not a playoff game. https://t.co/HjRyH5mAXA pic.twitter.com/j5lPe5LHXW

And, as it turns out, despite the fact that he returned at the end of August and performed as the lineup's top hitter during an otherwise sleepy stretch run to end the season, Anthony has been battling the hand the whole time. In fact, Andruw Monasterio had been informed before the game even started that he may be called on to replace Anthony in the lineup. "He took a check swing and then another swing and his hand flared on him. And it got uncomfortable, so we had to make a move there," Chad Tracy said. "It's difficult. You'll get a zinger every once in a while where you feel something, it's fine, it goes away … [Tuesday] some stuff happened that was more serious and was uncomfortable." (Alex Speier, Boston Globe)

Update, 4:20 PM: Anthony is not just out of the lineup tonight, he's out for the series:

Roman Anthony won't play again in this series and the Red Sox have petitioned to the league for a roster replacement, which would.also knock Roman out for the ALDS

Roman Anthony was driven back to Boston last night and had imaging that revealed multiple new strains in his hand plus a re-aggravation of the old injury. He is out for the foreseeable future.

Update, 5:30 PM: And just to make things a little weirder, Anthony will be replaced in the lineup by none other than Curtis Mead, who has effectively not played at all for the Red Sox this year due to injury.

With Anthony out, Jahmai Jones will DH and leadoff, while Nate Eaton will play left.

Red Sox lineup (no Roman Anthony) for Game 2 against the Yankees:

DH Jahmai Jones
C Adley Rutschman
1B Willson Contreras
RF Wilyer Abreu
CF Ceddanne Rafaela
3B Caleb Durbin
2B Nick Sogard
SS Trevor Story 
LF Nate Eaton 

RHP Sonny Gray

Anthony was hardly the only hitter to struggle against Cam Schlittler last night. And making matters worse was the fact that the Sox had been preparing to face him for weeks. But Schlittler had a surprise in store for the Sox, as he unleashed his curveball far more than he typically does. "He was landing it just for some get-me-overs to try to get back into counts and getting ahead early. Good on him to kinda mix it up there," said Caleb Durbin. "I thought he was doing a better job today of mixing up in the zone and lower in the zone with fastballs and his curveball." (Chris Cotillo, MassLive)

It won't matter how the lineup performs tonight if Sonny Gray can't keep the Yankees off the board. Gray has an ugly history with the Yankees. The arguable nadir of his career occurred during his brief time in pinstripes and he has since said he never wanted to play for the Yankees in the first place. But he doesn't necessarily regret his time in the Bronx. "I think there's a lot of people and a lot of players that can have one bump in the road and not get back on the tracks," he said, "and for me, there's been bumps along the way and that may have been a little bit of a bigger bump than others. But then to be able to recenter, to refocus, to continue to have confidence in yourself and not get off the wagon, get back on the wagon and continue to move forward in your career and in your life as well … ultimately it made me a better person." (Tara Sullivan, Boston Globe)

Ben Rice, unfortunately, did always want to play for the Yankees, despite the fact that he grew up in Cohasset and likely has an opinion on South Shore style bar pizza. But his New England roots aren't the only unusual thing about him, as he's also the rare Ivy League grad in the big leagues. (Ronald Blum, Boston.com)

Sonny's hatred of the Yankees is, of course, welcome around these parts. But it's possible that the Yankees are doing one thing in particular better than everyone else: constructing their roster for these short Wild Card round series. (Michael Baumann, FanGraphs)

But roster construction alone isn't going to win a playoff series, and this particular playoff series is not yet over. "I mean, I haven't heard the fat lady sing yet," Payton Tolle said last night. "So we're just going to keep going out there. I believe in us. So it's going to be fun to watch these guys compete tomorrow." (Christopher Smith, MassLive)

title: George Lombard Jr.'s late go-ahead homer punctuates Yankees' 6-4 comeback win over Rays
description: Cam Schlittler made his final start of a season worthy of the AL Cy Young, while George Lombard Jr. powered the Yankees to a 6-4 come-from-behind win over the rival Tampa Bay Rays.
fullText:
In the final game of their four-game home series against the Tampa Bay Rays (96-63), the Yankees (92-67) came back from 4-0 down to win 6-4.

-- In the second inning, after allowing a walk to Jonny DeLuca and a single to Richie Palacios with two outs away, Yankees starter Cam Schlittler struck out Ryan Vilade to strand Rays baserunners on first and third and preserve a scoreless tie.

-- The following inning, Taylor Walls drew a leadoff walk. Walls came around to score on the very next at-bat, a single by Yandy Diaz, which became an unearned RBI double when right fielder Heliot Ramos' throw to third base intended to tag out Walls skittered away. Then, Rays star third baseman Junior Caminero laced an RBI single to double the damage in the inning.

-- With the Rays having clinched the AL East division title, Yankees manager Aaron Boone made it clear that he would be limiting the number of pitches his starters throw during the team's remaining regular season games to ensure their arms are fresh for the postseason. Accordingly, with the Yanks still trailing 2-0, he pulled Schlittler for right-handed reliever Michael Fulmer, who opened the fourth inning with a clean frame to work with. Caminero knocked Fulmer out of the game with one out away in the fifth, mashing an RBI double off the left field wall, which scored Diaz. Tim Hill relieved Fulmer and worked into - and more importantly, out of - a bases-loaded jam to hold the Rays to their 3-0 lead.

-- With Luis Gil on the mound for the sixth inning, the Yankees couldn't complete a double play when Gil dropped George Lombard Jr.'s on-target throw to first base. A run scored as a result. In the bottom half of the frame, Austin Wells clubbed a solo homer to cut Tampa's lead to 4-1. Gil pushed onward to record a scoreless seventh inning.

-- Lombard singled home Ben Rice in the bottom of the seventh with a one-out double, before the shortstop added another run thanks to a wild pitch with an acrobatic slide-turned-hop-turned tag of home plate, beating out Rays catcher Liam Hicks. With two outs and Yankees baserunners on second and third, Paul Goldschmidt completed the comeback and tied the game, 4-4, with a single to center field. Cody Bellinger grounded out with runners on the corners to end the inning.

-- Rookie reliever Bradley Hanner handled the eighth for the Yankees. After allowing a leadoff double, he battled back to record a scoreless inning.

-- With the score still tied, one runner on base, and two outs in the inning, Lombard cranked a pitch down the left field line, a moonshot that stayed fair and gave New York a 6-4 lead.

-- Hanner closed the door in the ninth inning, earning his first career win as well as his first career save, sealing the series win for the Yankees, 6-4 the final on Thursday night.

-- Following his brief start on Thursday night, Schlittler's final stats for the 2026 regular season were set in stone. Across 33 starts, Schlittler pitched to the tune of a 1.95 ERA and 0.92 WHIP. He tallied 239 strikeouts and just 47 walks in 193.2 IP. Time will tell whether his sensational season is rewarded with the AL Cy Young Award.

The rookie shortstop was the hero on Thursday night. He tallied three RBI on two hits - a double and a two-run homer, his seventh in just 41 career games thus far - and showcased his athleticism on his improvisational slide, which allowed him to score from third on a wild pitch.

GEORGE LOMBARD JR. CLUTCH 2-RUN HOMER FOR THE LEAD! pic.twitter.com/c2nuoMyhqW

title: Yankees must start Carlos Rodón in potential Wild Card Game 3 against Red Sox
description: New York Yankees left-hander Carlos Rodón has been pitching well as the season winds down.
fullText:
The 2026 MLB season concludes on Sunday, with all 30 teams beginning play around 3 p.m. ET. The New York Yankees are one of six clubs to officially punch their ticket to the postseason so far and are 90-66 on the year.

The Yankees' superstar outfielder Aaron Judge only managed to appear in 66 games this season due first to a broken rib and now to a strained right calf. Even with Judge missing all the time he did, New York still won a good bit without him.

The problem is that they did not win quite enough, and will likely have to play in the Wild Card round as a result. The team is second place in the American League East, five games behind the Tampa Bay Rays with six to play (three against them).

The Yankees just concluded game one of four versus the Rays Tuesday afternoon in the first game of a split doubleheader. They won 2-0 on the back of eight shutout innings from lefty starter Carlos Rodón (7-3, 2.67 ERA).

There are still many possibilities, but in all likelihood the Yankees will host a best-of-three in the Wild Card versus their rival Boston Red Sox next week. Both teams are fairly locked into their seedings for the moment.

Seeing as they likely will not be, that would open the door for Rodón to pitch a Game 3 versus the Red Sox. Cole has famously struggled against them in his Yankee career, and Rodón has been on fire lately.

title: What is Yankees’ Aaron Judge facing? Surgeon weighs in on possible return, calf re-injury risk
description: A sports surgeon details when Yankees captain Aaron Judge might be able to return from a calf strain.
fullText:
NEW YORK — The Yankees surely were in a somber mood during Sunday night's cross-country flight from Phoenix to New York. The AL East race is all but over and Aaron Judge is hurt again, this time potentially for the season.

The Diamondbacks prevailed 5-3 on Saturday night and 8-4 on Sunday afternoon, costing the Yankees two more games in the standings and leaving them six games behind with seven games remaining in the regular season.

Following Monday's off day, the first-place Rays will be in the Bronx for four games in three days at Yankee Stadium, which will probably lead to champagne corks popping in the visiting clubhouse. The Rays need just one win to clinch the AL East.

At this point, the Yankees will inevitably face the Red Sox a week from Tuesday in Game 1 of a Wild Card Series.

The mystery is whether Judge will be back for this best-of-three.

1. The three-time MVP is back on the injured list with a right calf strain less than two weeks after returning from a fractured rib that sidelined him for 88 games.

2. The strain is in the soleus muscle.

3. He's eligible to be activated for next Sunday's regular-season finale, game 162.

How bad is it? What did the MRI reveal?

As usual, the Yankees and Judge have remained guarded/secretive about revealing his injury and rehab details.

"It doesn't matter what the grade is," manager Aaron Boone said last Friday in Phoenix. "We're going to get him back or we're not. That's what we're going to work to do and we'll see.''

Judge basically said the same thing to Yankees media on Saturday, while adding, "I'd like to be back for the playoffs. That's definitely the plan."

What can we unpack from what little we know?

NJ.com consulted with an NYU Langone Health sports orthopedic surgeon to provide a clearer picture of what Judge is facing without knowing if the strain is a Grade 1 (mild), Grade 2 (moderate partial tear) or Grade 3 (severe complete rupture).

"If it's a Grade 1, in two weeks you could see Judge doing baseball activities again and then three weeks back playing," Dr. Spencer Stein said. "It's a calf muscle strain and they're annoying injuries."

Judge was injured during last Wednesday's game in Minnesota, so three weeks would be Oct. 7. If the Yankees win their Wild Card Series, that would be Game 3 of their best-of-five Division Series with the Rays.

"But that's really best-case scenario," Dr. Stein said. "That would be the fastest."

Yankees designated hitter Giancarlo Stanton went on the IL in April with a Grade 1 calf strain and still hasn't returned. He had a setback in June, and then while rehabbing, he strained his other calf in August.

If Judge rushes back, he'd also be risking a setback, the doctor warned.

"I've seen studies there's up to 50% chance of re-injury in these muscular injuries — hamstring injuries, calf muscle injuries," Dr. Stein said. "There's a high rate of retear, so it's definitely a balance of not going back too quickly on them."

Rushing back might be why Judge is hurt again. When he was out with his rib injury, he was shut down from baseball activities from June 1 until Aug. 19. Less than three weeks later, Judge was back from the IL and playing right field for the Yankees with no rehab games and a few live batting-practice at-bats packed into a workout the day before his first game back.

"Well, I would say that there should always be a stepwise return to sports where you build things up and that takes time," Dr. Stein said. "When you're under a time constraint because it's end of season and the playoffs are around the corner, sometimes you have to take a risk and go a little faster. But with a risk, you can end up with another injury."

The location of his calf strain is problematic.

"The gastrocnemius, plantaris and soleus muscles comprise the calf, and the soleus muscle is a push-off muscle and part of the Achilles tendon," Dr. Stein said. "There's just a lot of force in that area, a lot of strain and stress, especially when you're swinging a baseball bat."

If Judge returns, he'd be much better off DHing instead of playing right field, Dr. Stein added.

"No question," he said. "The soleus muscle constantly is engaged during simple standing and walking."

That's another risk the Yankees would have to take.

Judge would have to play right field rather than be the designated hitter. Ben Rice, who has 39 home runs and 95 RBI, is entrenched at DH, while Luis Garcia Jr. and Paul Goldschmidt form a potent first base first-base platoon

Here is Dr. Stein's advice for Judge:

"Follow the instructions and take it day-by-day. Work with the therapists and trainers. Make sure your strength is there. You don't want to rush it too much. You don't want a long-term injury that keeps happening.

"You want to be able to come back, and we get that, but you do want to meet the criteria: Good strength with a good amount of flexibility in the knee and ankle area."

According to MLB insider Bob Nightengale of USA Today, Judge's injury has left the Yankees with "no idea" if he'll play again this season. Judge, a key to the Yankees' success this postseason, might be out for the rest of the year.

"The New York Yankees, who have played without All-Star outfielder Aaron Judge for most of the season, are bracing themselves now for the possibility that their three-time MVP may not play again the rest of the season," Nightengale writes. "... The Yankees have no idea whether he can play again this season."

Judge was out for a long time due to a rib issue, but returned in August with the hopes of being a contributor down the stretch. He didn't go through a rehab assignment and tried helping out at the big-league level right away.

Now, he's back on the IL due to a right calf strain and will miss 10 days at minimum, which would bring him to the end of the regular season.

He might come back in time for the playoffs, but there would likely be a lot of concern about his production if he does come back, as the questions about his health will be very real.

Aaron Boone told reporters recently, "I don't know," regarding whether Judge would play again or not. That's not the kind of update Yankees fans will like to hear.

Unfortunately, with the postseason just a few weeks away, Yankees fans should expect to be without Judge for quite a while, if not for the rest of the 2026 season, including the playoffs.

The Yankees, entering play on Saturday, September 19, are 89-64 and have clinched a postseason spot already. As they try to make up ground in the AL East race and begin the MLB playoffs, they're likely to do so with Judge, as his return is unknown.

fullText:
New York Mets' Bo Bichette has a decision to make this offseason. He can forgo the $42 million per season he's owed over the next two seasons ($84 million total) and opt out to become a free agent.

Bichette has been batting .263 with 152 hits, 16 home runs, 73 RBIs, and 72 runs scored in 146 games this season, per StatMuse. Nonetheless, the 28-year-old has been hitting .293 with 100 hits, 11 home runs, 45 RBIs, and 44 runs scored in 87 games for the Mets since June 1, per StatMuse.

With the Mets' 2026 season winding down and the team heading toward missing the playoffs for a second straight season, Patrick McAvoy of Fastball on SI believes Bichette will have suitors this offseason, including the New York Yankees and Toronto Blue Jays.

Starting with the Yankees, if Bichette wants to remain in New York, McAvoy sees a potential there in the Bronx.

"The New York Yankees are contenders right now, but they have some questions in the infield beyond the 2026 season. Jazz Chisholm Jr. will be a free agent," McAvoy wrote in a Sept. 11 article.

"George Lombard Jr. likely will be at shortstop. But what about third base? Ryan McMahon has one more season on his deal, but is batting .214. Bichette could help New York either at second base — if Chisholm leaves — or third base."

After a challenging start to the season, Bichette settled into New York. Would he really want to start over in a new city after finally getting comfortable in the Big Apple?

If Bichette does decide that New York isn't for him, McAvoy notes that a return to the Toronto Blue Jays would be ideal. Bichette hit .294 with 904 hits, 111 home runs, 437 RBIs, and 438 runs scored in 748 games during his time in Toronto, per StatMuse.

"The Blue Jays' lineup has been brutal so far this season," McAvoy added in his article. "In fact, the Blue Jays have been a disappointment in general after making it all the way to Game 7 of the World Series last year. Bichette struggled early on this year, but he's slashing .265/.317/.399 with a .716 OPS now, along with 16 homers and 73 RBIs in 144 games played.

"The 28-year-old turned his season around and would immediately make the Blue Jays' lineup better. Plus, these two sides certainly are familiar with one another after Bichette spent the first seven seasons of his career in Toronto. If Bichette opts out, a reunion makes too much sense."

Meanwhile, John Harper of SNY believes that Bichette should look to opt in, given that the infielder might not get $42 million per year over the next two years that are still left on his contract, per Spotrac. He could earn more than the $84 million remaining on his current deal, but he would need to sign a longer contract to do so.

"You've got the lockout coming," Harper said in a Sept. 11 video on SNY's YouTube channel. "You're not sure what the salary structure is going to look like, if there's a cap or not. I think that's part of it too. [Bichette] has been good since the terrible start, but I was looking at it, and he's not a superstar. He's a really good offensive player [and] has got an under .800 OPS in the second half, when he's done most of his best hitting.

"He doesn't hit for a lot of power [and] he's been a clutch guy again since the bad start, hitting almost .300 with runners in scoring position. To me, [$84 million] for the next two years; you can go out in the market after that [but] you're not getting [$42 million] a year anymore. Now you're getting a longer contract, but I would stick it out for these two years and then maybe take my chance."

title: Where Mets’ Nolan McLean stands in Rookie of the Year race after Subway Series clunker
description: Mets right-hander Nolan McLean gave up a career-high 10 hits in Friday night's loss to the Yankees at Yankee Stadium.
fullText:
NEW YORK — Mets right-hander Nolan McLean took the mound on Friday night at Yankee Stadium as a long shot in the race for the Rookie of the Year Award in the National League.

It was always going to be an uphill climb for him to catch Cincinnati's Sal Stewart, but with a dominant outing against the Yankees, McLean could've taken his case to contend for that prize to another level of legitimacy.

After all, McLean entered play Friday with the fourth-best ERA of any starting pitcher in baseball — not just rookies — since May 25 (2.24). Overall, his 3.06 ERA across 28 starts this year ranked ninth among qualified arms in the National League. Only six other pitchers had more strikeouts than McLean in 2026 (179).

Rather than building more momentum, however, McLean put together a loss that featured one of his worst lines of the year with a few firsts.

McLean gave up five earned runs against the Yankees in a 6-4 loss on a career-high 10 hits over five frames. Cody Bellinger's three-run home run off McLean in the second inning came on a curveball from McLean with two strikes, the first homer he's allowed on that pitch in his big-league career.

While that home run swing from Bellinger was a tip-the-cap moment — McLean wasn't unhappy with the spot at the knees — interim manager Andy Green pointed out postgame that McLean could've done a better job using the entire zone. There were too many pitches that the right-hander left out and over the plate, pitches that the Yankees pounced on early and often.

"Nolan had the opportunity to probably attack in more than he did today," Green said. "You could feel from the beginning [the Yankees] were living out over [the plate]. So it wasn't necessarily his best day. There was opportunity to probably get in more aggressively than he did."

On one hand, that's frustrating for the Mets to see McLean struggle with hitting spots and attacking with his electric stuff. McLean has recognized this summer that his clunkers often correspond to outings where he doesn't execute well enough with hitting his spots or he fails to get ahead in counts.

That said, even with Friday's dud, McLean has been a top starter in the league for the last several months and he clearly has more room to improve heading into next season. His overall numbers this season are still elite, too. McLean now ranks 16th among all qualified starters in ERA (3.24 over 29 starts). His five strikeouts on Friday pushed McLean up to 184 on the season which is 13th in MLB (three ahead of Paul Skenes and two behind Jacob deGrom). Only seven starters have a lower opponents batting average than McLean (.212). All of that should make Mets fans even more encouraged about what McLean's sophomore season will look like, regardless of where he finishes in the Rookie of the Year Award race.

title: Bill Madden: Tampa Bay Rays ready to usher in new era with stadium relocation near
description: NEW YORK — For years baseball people have marveled at the Tampa Bay Rays’ ability to remain competitive in the American League East despite consistently low industry payrolls and annual attendance. fullText:
NEW YORK — For years baseball people have marveled at the Tampa Bay Rays' ability to remain competitive in the American League East despite consistently low industry payrolls and annual attendance. Since 2008, the Rays have been to the postseason nine times, including the World Series twice, always with payrolls of well over $100 million less than the Yankees.

At the same time, Tampa Bay fans have gotten used to the Rays' jettisoning their favorite players (See: Isaac Paredes, Randy Arozarena, Brandon Lowe and Tyler Glasnow in just the last three years) as soon as they became too costly or near free agency. And with the clock continuing to tick on their expiring (2028) lease at dreary Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, Fla., there's never been a sense of permanence of the Rays in Tampa Bay.

Recently, both the Tampa city council and the Hillsborough County commissioners voted to approve a new $2.3 billion mixed-use stadium project near Hillsborough College's Dale Mabry Boulevard campus, not far from Raymond James Stadium, the home of the NFL Tampa Bay Bucs. The plan is similar to what the Atlanta Braves constructed in Cobb County, Ga., in 2015 for a stadium surrounded by a village of shops and restaurants that would produce addition revenue for the team.

It was always the accepted view of most folks in the Tampa Bay area that if the Rays were going to survive they would have to be in Tampa where the large majority of their 3 1/2 million residents are. This was part of the reason the Rays have remained one of the top revenue sharing recipients in baseball, an average of nearly $60 million a year. That's on top of the $50 million they and the other 29 clubs receive annually from the MLB Central Fund. So they've had the money to increase payroll, but the previous Rays owner Stu Sternberg just chose not to spend it.

If the owners are able to establish a cap in the new collective bargaining agreement, revenue sharing would go away, but the Rays are anticipating revenues of far more than $60 million from the new park and surrounding village which is now slated to be ready by 2029. For sure, now that the stadium issue has finally been resolved, the Rays, under their new ownership led by Jacksonville developer Patrick Zalupski, are expected to be operating vastly different. Last week Zalupski told the Tampa Bay Times: "Tampa's the No. 11 media market in the country. There's nothing holding it back, "adding that with the new ballpark and the development around it, "we should be able to drive payroll (currently 27th at $116,208,358) into the top 15 circle and maybe even the top 10."

In the meantime, the Rays have been leading the American League East since June 27, but will be facing their biggest challenge now in the September stretch, starting with this present road trip through Texas where they snapped a 10-game skid at Globe Life Field as of Friday, and three in Atlanta against the Braves. They then finish the season with three games with the Red Sox, four in New York with the Yankees and three more at home with the Phillies.

That four-game series at Yankee Stadium Sept. 22-24 figures to be the biggest regular-season series for both the Rays and the Yankees in years, especially since the Yankees expect to be (Aaron Judge) whole, while Rays GM Eric Neander made significant upgrades to his pitching at the trade deadline with Freddy Peralta from the Mets and hard-throwing righty reliever Tyler Wells from the Orioles, and in perhaps the best acquisition of all, filled the Rays longstanding need — a catcher who can hit — by landing Liam Hicks from the Marlins

If the Rays are able to emerge through that gauntlet still atop the AL East it should be cause for considerable concern for the Yankees. Because as improved as they've become this year, they figure to be this good and better for years to come with one of the top player development systems in baseball with a half dozen top 100 prospects including outfielders Theo Gillen, Jake Melton and Austin Overn and catcher Caden Bodine, all of whom could be making their debuts at some point next year.

In every way, the baseball future couldn't be brighter in Tampa Bay.

title: Yankees place Trent Grisham on IL with hamstring strain, recall Jasson Domínguez
description: The Yankees’ center fielder will miss some time after being pulled from Friday night’s game.
fullText:
The Yankees lost in walk-off fashion to San Diego on Friday night, but they might not have played extras had it not been for a misplay that allowed the Padres to score their only run of the initial nine innings. With two outs in the second, Xander Bogaerts got under a pitch from Max Fried on what could charitably be described as a flare to center. It was a ball that most center fielder would've at minimum come close to and have the chance for a diving catch.

But for the Yankees, Trent Grisham was in center field, and while he was once an elite defender, he has been far from that in 2026. It didn't help that he was playing a guy with an 82 OPS+ and only 11 homers far too deep, but regardless, he was clearly not moving well on the play. The ball dipped in with ease and Ty France scored. When the half-inning ended, Grisham spoke to the team trainer and disappeared down the dugout tunnel. Soon, the Yankees announced that Grisham was dealing with discomfort in his right hamstring, the same one that sent him to the IL earlier in 2026. It's been an uneven year on the whole for Grisham, who has hit .211/.308/.395 with 18 homers but only a 95 OPS+.

Now, we know that Grisham is indeed heading back to the IL. Jasson Domínguez will fly from Scranton to San Diego to rejoin the team and take Grisham's spot on the roster. The former top prospect had an injury of his own earlier in 2026, but when given the chance to play, he did not acquit himself well, batting just .230/.270/.380 with a 79 OPS+ and exactly 0.0 rWAR.

It might only be a short-term stay for Domínguez since it seems like Aaron Judge is tracking to return to the team soon (though New York has made no announcements) and there's only so much roster flexibility at the moment. But for now, Domínguez will serve as outfield depth, though Spencer Jones will likely get the lion's share of time in center with Grisham out. Cody Bellinger is a candidate for some center field time as well, though he did bang himself up a bit on a foul ball last night too.

Prior to today’s game, the Yankees made the following roster moves:
•Placed OF Trent Grisham on the 10-day injured list with a right hamstring strain.
•Recalled OF Jasson Domínguez (#24) from Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre.

title: Yankees’ Cam Schlittler makes MLB history, joining Randy Johnson as only other pitcher to accomplish feat
description: Cam Schlittler continues to be a revelation.
fullText:
New York Yankees starting pitcher Cam Schlittler has accomplished something rarely seen on an MLB mound.

He joins Randy Johnson as the only modern-era pitcher to produce a streak of this length while striking out more batters than hits allowed on the road.

MORE: Yankees, Aaron Boone announce new pitching plans for weekend series in San Diego

Aug 21, 2026; Bronx, New York, USA; New York Yankees starting pitcher Cam Schlittler (31) pitches against the Toronto Blue Jays during the first inning at Yankee Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Brad Penner-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)

Schlittler delivered another dominant performance in the Yankees' 6-3 victory over the Los Angeles Angels last night. The right-hander struck out nine batters while allowing just two hits across eight innings, continuing what has become an extraordinary run away from New York.

With his latest outing, Schlittler has now recorded more strikeouts than hits allowed in each of his last 21 road starts. The streak dates back to August 2, 2025, and during that span, the Yankees sophomore has struck out 157 batters while surrendering only 70 hits.

That puts Schlittler in rare company. The only other pitcher in the modern era to achieve a streak of at least this length was Johnson, who accomplished the feat across 23 games with the Arizona Diamondbacks from 1999 to 2000.

MORE: Padres made a huge mistake & are paying for it now

Schlittler's historic road stretch is just one part of an impressive sophomore campaign. The Yankees starter has emerged as a legitimate contender for the American League Cy Young Award, posting a 2.04 ERA and 0.94 WHIP alongside a 12-6 record through 29 starts.

His consistency has also played a major role in keeping the Yankees firmly in the American League playoff picture. New York currently holds the first Wild Card spot with an 80-60 record and a 9.5-game cushion.

The Yankees will now turn their attention toward a weekend series in San Diego against the Padres. With Schlittler continuing to pitch at an elite level, New York has another major weapon as it looks to secure its postseason position.

If his historic road dominance continues, Schlittler could finish the season not only as one of the Yankees' most important players, but also as one of the American League's premier starting pitchers.

title: Angels’ Outfield Depth in Trouble After Josh Lowe Injury Scratch
description: The Los Angeles Angels scratched outfielder Josh Lowe from Wednesday's game against the New York Yankees with neck stiffness. The post Angels’ Outfield Depth in Trouble After Josh Lowe Injury Scratch appeared first on LA Sports Report.
fullText:
The Los Angeles Angels scratched outfielder Josh Lowe from Wednesday's game against the New York Yankees with neck stiffness.

The Angels' outfield is severely lacking in depth, as they currently have just four outfielders listed on their active roster—one of whom is Lowe. Wade Meckler will move over to right field to cover for Lowe, with Jose Siri getting the start in left field.

Lowe, an offseason acquisition from the Tampa Bay Rays, has been with the Angels for nearly the entire season, only being away from the team during a month-long stint in Triple-A. He can play any position across the outfield, providing valuable depth in each position for the Halos.

The 28-year-old has 10 homers on the year, driving in 27 runs through 95 games this season. He has a .625 OPS this season, which would be the lowest mark of his career if he finishes the season at this pace.

His best stretch of baseball came after the Angels recalled him from Triple-A in June, where he went 8-for-18 through his final six games of June. He hit a homer and drove in four runs during that stretch, posting an OPS north of 1.000 during his hot streak.

Siri, Meckler and Mike Trout are the only other players explicitly listed as outfielders on the Angels' roster, though they have other players who could stand in if needed.

Other than Lowe, Siri, Meckler and Trout, the Angels have a few options if they need to bring someone into the outfield later in the year.

Kyren Paris came up from Triple-A Tuesday for the Angels' September call-ups, and he has plenty of experience in the outfield despite primarily playing in the middle of the infield. 2024 first-round pick Christian Moore also primarily plays in the infield, but the Angels tested him out in left field when they called him up earlier in the season.

Lastly, Adam Frazier has spent some time in the outfield this season for the Angels, and could fill in if needed.

Even still, the Angels' outfield is running extremely thin, and remains an area they'll have to reinforce come the offseason.
