title: Yankees Birthday of the Day: Foster Edwards
description: Edwards made the big leagues when he was just 21. The rest of his career didn’t go well.
fullText:
If the name Foster Edwards doesn't immediately inspire awe in your mind, are you really a Yankees fan? Just kidding. Edwards, a right-handed pitcher, was a Yankee for all of two games in 1930, and he didn't really do anything to ensure that his name would be etched onto history during those appearances.

Yet he was a Yankee all the same, and as a writer for the Internet's most devoted (citation needed) Yankees fan site, I will try my darnedest to celebrate his birthday and career. After all, he was the only player in franchise history to be born on September 1st, and here we are at the outset of September! It's Foster's lucky day.

Foster Hamilton "Eddie" Edwards
Born: September 1, 1903 (Holstein, IA)
Died: January 4, 1980 (Barnstable, MA)
Yankees Tenure: 1930

Long before Ben Rice stepped onto a diamond and even prior to 1930s standout third baseman Red Rolfe, it was Edwards who became the first former Dartmouth standout to play for the Yankees. Following his graduation from Central High School in Hennepin, Minnesota, Edwards pitched at Dartmouth from 1924-25 and stayed in New England for the beginning of his pro career. Edwards recorded a 4.02 ERA in 112 innings across 21 games for the Worcester Panthers of the Eastern League, and 1925 also saw him make his MLB debut.

When Edwards toed the rubber for the Boston Braves on July 2, 1925, he was still just 21 years old. His task was to mop up a game where the Braves were already losing 15-2 to the Brooklyn Robins in the seventh inning. He managed to finish the game, but that was about where the positives ended. He gave up five runs (two earned) on six hits and a walk. That was his only appearance in the majors that year.

To his credit, Edwards put together a very strong campaign in 1926, albeit mainly for the Providence Rubes, who had succeeded Worcester in the Eastern League. He went 25-8 with a 2.95 ERA across 259 innings, leading the EL in wins. He would return to the major leagues in September, going 2-0 with a 0.72 in three starts and 25 innings pitched. It seemed like he was poised to take bigs by storm.

Alas, that did not happen. The following year, Edwards went 2-8 with a 4.99 ERA as the Braves relegated him to relief duty in the latter half of the season. His struggles continued in 1928, and after the season, he decided to retire and enter the grocery business. However, Edwards evidently wasn't quite ready to give up, and the Yankees must have seen something in him, as they picked him up prior to the 1930 season.

The 26-year-old impressed the club in spring training and was on the roster early that year, alongisde luminaries like Babe Ruth and Lou Gehrig. Maybe in an alternate universe, Edwards might have rewarded the Yankees handsomely, playing a role on those fabled 1930s squads and carving out a name for himself in pinstriped lore.

That didn't come to pass in this one, though. Edwards gave up four runs in 1.2 innings of work across two early season relief appearances, and that was all the Yankees needed to see before effectively banishing him to the minors. And that was all she wrote.

Sometimes—heck, most times—the things you set your heart on don't work out. I'm sure Edwards had bigger aspirations for his career—why else would he have returned to pitch for the Yanks after spending an entire year out of pro ball? But it just didn't happen. He tried, though, and I think that's a legacy worth hanging your hat on — to have tried something with your whole heart. That counts, even if you don't get what you want in the end.

Happy birthday, Foster. Rest easy.

title: “Stay Out Of That” – Aaron Judge Goes Off On Red Sox Broadcaster After Incendiary Comments About Jazz Chisholm Jr. & Austin Wells

fullText:

"He needs to stay out of that and not be telling people to throw at players and injure players. That's not what this game's about. That game determines home field advantage in the playoffs. It's a six-run game. They get a couple guys on and hit a big homer, all of a sudden, we're getting our bullpen guys up and in a tight spot," Judge said.

"If you're not going to hold him on, what's going on here? Are you conceding, not conceding? What's going on? It's a six-run game. It's still a close ballgame. So yeah, not too happy hearing a broadcaster is talking about trying to injure and hurt a player. He needs to clean that up," he added.

"He's doing well. He's here, you know. He's here to kind of continue to ramp up baseball activities. So, you know, we're getting closer, but feel good about where he's at. I think it's possible. I'm not going to put a date on it, but, you know, I think those things are in play now. It's, again, about getting the durability and the workload built up on him, which is the biggest thing now," Boone said.

fullText:
NEW YORK — Aaron Judge is set to join the Yankees on this week's West Coast road trip as he continues to work his way back from a broken rib.

Judge has been progressing through baseball activities — including throwing from 100 feet and taking indoor, overhand batting practice — but had not yet faced high-velocity pitching.

"I'm sure he'll be ramped up and a lot more involved in the pregame stuff," manager Aaron Boone said Sunday of the plan for Judge on the road trip.

"Hopefully out there, [Judge will] start to get on velocity and things like that, be part of the pregame stuff, and just get more entrenched into getting ready to come back."

The Yankees are set to begin a three-game series against the Los Angeles Angels in Anaheim on Monday, then play the Padres in San Diego over the weekend.

They have not shared a timeline for Judge to return, but with the Yankees in the thick of a playoff race, the slugger said last week that he would prefer to forgo a minor-league rehab assignment.

"Why waste at-bats?" Judge, 34, said Thursday. "Why waste anything down in a minor-league game? I've been doing this for a while now, and I've got a sense of what I need to do on the field and how to manage it, so why waste at-bats in Double-A or Triple-A?"

Judge has been sidelined since May 31 due to a right rib stress fracture — an injury he suspects occurred more than a month earlier when he dove in right field during a game in Houston.

The three-time American League MVP is hitting .248 with 17 home runs and a .907 OPS in 59 games this season. In his absence, Spencer Jones and Heliot Ramos are sharing time in right field.

In 2023, Judge didn't play in any minor-league rehab games before returning from a toe injury that had kept him out for about two months.

There are four weeks remaining in the regular season.

"I'm gonna play smart," Judge said last week. "I'm gonna still try to go out there and make every play I can, but you gotta be smart, especially near the end of the year now. You know, if it's Game 7 of the World Series, I'll definitely be diving, so I don't think that'll ever change. But just be smart the next couple weeks as we get back, and we'll be good."

title: Hall of Famer survived Yankees owner George Steinbrenner: ’I'll never reclaim those years'
description: MLB legend Dave Winfield is hoping to inspire others to stand strong with his new book.
fullText:
New Yankees owner George Steinbrenner tried everything to break him and destroy his reputation to the point of no return, but Dave Winfield refused to let him win.

Winfield stood up to the most powerful owner in baseball, fought back just like he has throughout life, and now proudly tells his story with a book – and soon, a documentary.

It will not attract splashy headlines and have the internet buzzing. It won't make former teammates and managers uncomfortable with secrets that are unveiled. It instead provides a deep emotional dive into the man himself.

Winfield insisted from the start of the hour-long interview with USA TODAY Sports that for everyone who thinks they really know him, once you read "Touching All the Bases: A Story of Power, Purpose, and Surviving the Bronx," you'll find out that you really didn't know him.

Winfield poured his heart and soul into the book, which was nearly six years in the making, and will be released Sept. 15.

He talks about life as a Black athlete going against one of the most powerful men in sports in Steinbrenner, details the heartache and stress of court battles with a woman from his past, the pain of the George Floyd murder in Minneapolis across the river where he grew up in St. Paul, working in the players union and his frustration with former players who are part of commissioner Rob Manfred's ambassador program, performance-enhancing drugs, personal tragedy, his bout with prostate cancer, his philanthropic foundation, flying out of New York City the morning of the terrorist attacks and his heartbreaking trip to Ground Zero.

"I've had a unique life, legacy and experience, and I have a unique story to tell," Winfield says. "My life experience is so different than what most people would imagine. I'm in the seventh inning of life, so it's time to tell it.

"If you've got a unique experience or story, I believe you've got to share it with people."

The experience, as he details in his book: "My experience as a Black man who went to war with one of the most powerful owners in sports tells an essential story, not just about the triumphs and challenges of my own career, but about the dynamics of race and power in America."

Winfield, 74, isn't comparing himself to Jackie Robinson or Curt Flood, but no one else comes to mind in the past 50 years in baseball who was more tormented and mistreated, but courageously fought back, becoming a first-ballot Hall of Fame player and one of the most well-respected athletes in the sports world.

He survived Steinbrenner's attempts to bring ruin him, but in the end, it was Steinbrenner who went down, receiving a lifetime suspension that was reduced to 2 ½ years for hiring a gambler in a failed attempt to destroy Winfield's reputation.

"I could have been really vengeful, hateful, disrespectful, unhappy, for all of the things that were thrown at me," Winfield says. "But that never happened. I won't say I didn't have bruises and was bent a little bit, but I didn't break.

"When I think about my career, people will say was quite successful, but I don't really know how good I could have been at the pinnacle of my career if I had been supported. I think I would have been a better player."

It was when the world was shut down from COVID in 2020 that Winfield was home, watching the horrifying footage of George Floyd being strangled on the streets by a Minneapolis police officer, that he knew it was time to tell his story.

"I had something that George Floyd and so many other Black people didn't," Winfield writes, "a voice. A chance to speak, to be heard, and to defend myself. Too many people don't have that chance. I hope those coming up today keep the pressure on our leaders and stand alongside the 'old heads' who have fought through past struggles for equality.

"I hope they refuse to relent too soon and push tirelessly for real transformation."

Winfield can't wait now to meet and shake the hands of Kwanza Jones, who became the first Black majority owner of a baseball team when she and her husband, Jose E. Feliciano, purchased the San Diego Padres, his first team. It has been a long time coming, but finally, history was made.

"It would have been nice to see it sooner,'' Winfield says, "but it doesn't surprise me that it hasn't happened before now. I'm just happy it has happened now."

Winfield, who once was interested in being part of an ownership group himself, has plenty to share to whoever wants to listen. No other player in baseball history had such a highly publicized feud with his team owner, and lived to tell about it, with the owner being the one who was suspended from the game.

It was nasty. It was revolting. It was public.

"Those disputes weren't just about money," said Winfield, who signed a historic 10-year, $23 million contract with the Yankees, "they were about power. It was an owner, speaking for all the others, making sure a player knew his place."

Despite years without speaking after his departure, with Steinbrenner irate and canceling plans to retire his number after Winfield chose to wear a Padres cap cap into the Hall of Fame, Winfield's wife, Tonya, convinced him to see Steinbrenner perhaps for the final time. Winfield took a six-hour flight to Tampa in July 2008, two years before Steinbrenner died.

"I decided to make the trip," Winfield said, "hoping it might help quite some of the angry thought that had been pin-balling around my head for decades. …. When I saw him, it was clear he wasn't well. His handshake had weakened. He struggled for words and could barely speak above a whisper. I could see he didn't have the strength or clarity to have an in-depth conversation about our past."

They spoke for 90 minutes. It started with a handshake. It ended with a hug.

"Did the meeting give me a sense of reconciliation, closure, or validation?" Winfield said. "To some extent it did, but I'll never reclaim those years of anguish.''

Winfield, who spent 12 years as a special assistant in the players union before retiring last spring, is proud of playing a major role with the union. He has seen the union's power evolve from the first time he put on his first MLB uniform 53 years ago, going straight from the University of Minnesota to the big leagues with the Padres.

There was no free agency in 1973. No salary arbitration. The minimum salary was $16,000. Most players had second jobs in the winter.

Now, the average MLB salary is $5.34 million, with two players – Juan Soto and Shohei Ohtani – receiving free-agent contracts worth at least $700 million. Winfield made about $28 million his entire career, which is $32 million less than Dodgers right fielder Kyle Tucker is earning just this year.

"I expect the owners will do whatever necessary to get what they want," Winfield writes, "including fighting dirty and impugning reputations. I know from personal experience how dirty the fight can get. We must stand strong in defense of our hard-earned rights."

Winfield, the first of four Hall of Famers from his hometown of St. Paul – with Jack Morris, Paul Molitor and Joe Mauer – talks about being a proud Minnesotan, where he was honored in May with St. Paul erecting a statue of him in the Dunning Sports Complex. He played every sport growing up, and was drafted by four teams in three sports in 1973. The Padres selected him with the fourth pick in the draft, the fifth round by the Atlanta Hawks of the NBA and the sixth round by the Utah Stars in the ABA, and the Minnesota Vikings in the 17th round.

"Believe me, I tell many parents now to allow your kids to play other sports," Winfield said. "You're seeing these kids get injured or burnt out by playing one sport. Coaches want to dominate all of their time with one sport. Let them be kids."

Winfield, who begins his book tour on Sept. 8 with an appearance on "Good Morning America'' and "The View'' the following day, hopes that his book and an upcoming documentary will help inspire those facing their own adversity.

"I'm an outlier how you approach things in life,'' Winfield says. "I've never been afraid to travel, go outside, never afraid to meet new people. There are a lot of people that would roll up in a ball and quit if they faced all the negative stuff coming my way. I overcame really significant odds, ugly situations and a lot of adversity. I went through it all and came out Ok on the other end.

title: Yankees sign former Mets top prospect Jarred Kelenic to minor-league deal
description: Kelenic played for the White Sox and Rangers earlier this season before being designated for assignment.
fullText:
The New York Yankees need outfield help with Aaron Judge's return still uncertain. They're looking to a former top major-league prospect for a possible contribution, one who also hopes he can revive his career with a postseason contender.

The Yankees have signed outfielder Jarred Kelenic to a minor-league deal, MLB.com's Bryan Hoch reports. He will report to the team's Triple-A affiliate in Scranton/Wilkes-Barre, the team announced on Saturday.

Kelenic, 27, was designated for assignment by the Texas Rangers last week. He compiled a .373/.447/.655 with their Triple-A affiliate and slashed .200/.333/.200 in 17 games with the major-league team.

Additionally, Kelenic spent time with the Chicago White Sox this season. He had a .202/.346/.464 slash line with their Triple-A club and hit .226 with a .626 OPS in 19 big-league games.

JARRED KELENIC CALLS BALLGAME! pic.twitter.com/oh6tjno0n1

Kelenic was originally the 2018 first-round pick (No. 6 overall) by the New York Mets out of Waukesha West High School in Wisconsin. He was traded to the Seattle Mariners later that year with four other players in exchange for Robinson Canó and Edwin Díaz.

After three disappointing seasons with a .204 average and .656 OPS, the Mariners traded Kelenic to the Atlanta Braves. But the former top prospect still didn't fulfill his potential with the Braves (.222, .660 OPS) and opted for free agency rather than go to the minors after the 2025 campaign.

A left-handed hitter who can play all three outfield positions, Kelenic could possibly provide depth on the Yankees roster behind Cody Bellinger, Trent Grisham and Spencer Jones. (And Judge, if he's able to return.) Jasson Domínguez and Yanquiel Fernández will likely be in the outfield mix as well.

Judge is "closer" to returning from his right rib stress fracture and could soon begin hitting off a high-velocity machine. If that goes well, the reigning American League MVP doesn't want to go on a minor-league rehab assignment, but be activated to the major-league roster right away.

"Why waste at-bats?" Judge said to reporters on Thursday. Yankees manager Aaron Boone said that decision will be made by the organization.

Without Judge, the Yankees have hit a collective .219 with a .674 OPS and scored 292 runs since June 1. During the first two months of the season, they scored 305 runs.

title: Red Sox Answer Offensive Drought With Statement Shutout Win Over Yankees
description: The Red Sox ended their offensive drought early before their pitching staff completely silenced the Yankees in a much-needed bounce-back victory.
fullText:
Red Sox Answer Offensive Drought With Statement Shutout Win Over Yankees originally appeared on NESN. 

The Boston Red Sox finally broke through at the plate Saturday afternoon. Once they did, their pitching staff made certain the New York Yankees never had an opportunity to respond.

Boston bounced back from consecutive shutout losses with a 6-0 win over New York in the first game of Saturday's doubleheader at Yankee Stadium. Wilyer Abreu ended the Red Sox's scoreless drought in the opening inning, launching a two-out solo home run off Yankees starter Carlos Rodón. It was Abreu's 23rd homer of the season and gave Boston its first run since Wednesday.

That one swing ultimately provided more than enough support for Hunter Bennett and the Red Sox bullpen.

Bennett delivered six scoreless innings, allowing only three hits without issuing a walk. He struck out seven and threw 59 of his 83 pitches for strikes, producing a game score of 73. New York never sent more than four batters to the plate in any inning against Bennett. Its best opportunity came in the fourth when Heliot Ramos doubled, but Ceddanne Rafaela threw out Amed Rosario at home plate to preserve the shutout.

It was exactly the type of response Boston needed after its offense disappeared in consecutive losses.

The Red Sox entered Saturday looking for something positive after suffering back-to-back shutouts, including a 1-0 loss to the Yankees in Friday's series opener.

Shut ‘em out.

FINAL: #RedSox 6, Yankees 0#DirtyWater￼ pic.twitter.com/6GivFTAXpu

Abreu immediately removed the possibility of another scoreless afternoon, but Boston's pitching staff remained the biggest story. Bennett retired the final six batters he faced before handing the game to the bullpen. Tayron Guerrero worked around a seventh-inning single, Garrett Whitlock pitched a perfect eighth and Jovani Morán closed the game.

The four Boston pitchers combined to allow four hits and no walks while striking out nine.

Boston added its second run in the fifth when Adley Rutschman scored on a passed ball. The Red Sox then turned a close game into a comfortable victory with four runs in the ninth.

Andruw Monasterio drove home Caleb Durbin and Rutschman with a single. Nick Sogard followed with an RBI double before Rafaela completed the scoring with a run-producing single. Rutschman finished 3-for-4 with two runs, while Sogard went 2-for-4 with a double, an RBI and a run scored. Boston collected nine hits and went 3-for-8 with runners in scoring position.

The victory improved the Red Sox to 74-61 and pulled them within two games of the Yankees, who dropped to 76-59. It also evened the four-game series at one win apiece.

Boston will not have much time to celebrate. The Red Sox and Yankees return to the field Saturday night for the second half of their doubleheader. First pitch is scheduled for 6:15 p.m. ET at Yankee Stadium, with the game airing nationally on FOX.

After being shut out twice, Boston now has a chance to leave Saturday with two wins and make the American League East race significantly more interesting.

title: Red Sox Face Daunting Doubleheader Challenge Against Yankees Aces

fullText:

Fried's return comes exactly 15 days after the Yankees placed him on the injured list, allowing him to return following a minimum-length absence. The timing presents another difficult test for Boston's struggling lineup.

Boston went 0-for-9 with runners in scoring position and stranded 10 runners. The loss extended its scoreless streak to 18 innings.

Rodón and Fried give the Yankees a pair of accomplished left-handed starters for a doubleheader with significant American League playoff implications.

Fried will return to the rotation for the nightcap after initially expressing hope that his injured-list stay would be brief. The Yankees confirmed his scheduled start following Friday's victory, according to Pinstripe Alley.

The Red Sox first must deal with Rodón.

Boston will send Early to the mound in the opener and likely will need another strong pitching performance after wasting Patrick Sandoval's excellent start Friday. Sandoval allowed only one run on three hits over 5 1/3 innings, but Paul Goldschmidt's solo home run was enough to decide the game.

title: Yankees Announce Decision on Former Top 10 Prospect Before Astros Game

fullText:
The New York Yankees send their ace, Gerrit Cole, to the mound Thursday â weather permitting â to try to nail down a series win against the American League West-leading Houston Astros, after the two teams split the first two contests of the three-game set.

With the Boston Red Sox idle, the Yankees have a chance to push their lead in the race for the top AL Wild Card spot to three full games over their arch-rivals.

Before the Astros game, the Yankees announced a decision on a roster move with one of their most prized pitching prospects, who only last year ranked as No. 9 in the New York system, per MLB Pipeline, before an arm injury requiring surgery set him back.

That pitcher is Chase Hampton, and Thursday's roster move had nothing to do with a new injury. The Yankees' Double-A affiliate activated the right-hander from the temporarily inactive list on August 27, 2026, according to MiLB.com's transaction records, ending an 18-day gap and returning him to Somerset's rotation. The move landed alongside other Double-A moves, including the promotions of Trent Sellers and Harrison Cohen from Triple-A and the assignment of Luis Velasquez to High-A Hudson Valley.

Hampton had been placed on the temporarily inactive list on August 9, according to the Somerset Patriots' team social media account. The designation typically covers short absences outside a standard injured list stint â family matters, personal circumstances, a brief developmental pause â rather than a new physical setback, and nothing in the transaction record points to a fresh injury.

GettyChase Hampton #86 of the New York Yankees.

Hampton's entire 2026 season has been about recovery. He underwent Tommy John surgery on his right elbow in February 2025, an operation that wiped out that whole campaign and followed a spring bullpen session that left him in discomfort, according to a CBS Sports report.

The rehab assignment stretched across three levels this year, from Single-A Tampa on May 8 to High-A Hudson Valley on May 26 to Somerset on June 12. The results since the return have been rough â an 0-6 record with an 8.19 ERA across 48.1 innings in 2026, according to Baseball Savant data, including a 9.93 ERA over nine starts at Double-A before this month's inactive-list stint.

His rise looked fast before the injuries piled up. In his 2023 professional debut, Hampton posted a 3.63 ERA with 145 strikeouts across 106.2 innings between High-A Hudson Valley and Double-A Somerset, pushing him as high as the organization's No. 4 overall prospect on some boards behind a fastball that touched 99 mph, plus a slider and curveball scouts have praised.

New York added him to the 40-man roster in November 2025, protecting him from the Rule 5 Draft. Adams described him at the time as a prospect who could pitch his way into a late-2026 look if he stayed healthy, though he called Hampton "a more realistic 2027 rotation candidate."

The Renegades have an under the radar prospect who isn't on any of their top 30 rankings. Jackson Lovich was leading the Florida State League in homers when he was promoted to High A on July 28 and he's off to a great start with Hudson Valley, batting .343 in six games counting his 1-for-4 with a three-run homer in Tuesday night's 10-5 win at Jersey Shore.

Here are scouting reports on the Renegades' top three hitting prospects from manager Aaron Bossi:

The skinny: Switched to catching this season after playing outfield for Low A Tampa in 2025 (11 games LF, 5 games RF). … Had a two-hit, four-RBI game in a Monday night win at Jersey Shore. … Batting .276 with 12 homers against right-handed pitching and .217 with no homers versus lefties. … 18.6 strikeout percentage, 13.1 walk percentage. … Drexel Hill, Pa. native was a four-year starter at Rhode Island and hit .367 as a senior. … Ranks in top five in Rhode Island's career leaders for homers, RBI, doubles and walks. … Mother played basketball at Rider.

Manager Aaron Bossi's take: "We told Eric right after our A ball season last year that we were moving him to catcher. He caught in 2022 at Rhode Island for a few games, but it wasn't much at all. We made the change because we saw the offensive profile and thought this could maximize Eric's value. That transition from outfield was intriguing because he had a good arm out there. So now it's about moving like a catcher, shortening up the release, quickening up the feet. While the stolen bases stat doesn't look great right now, we are seeing real-time gains in how quickly he's been able to release the ball and how accurately he's able to deliver it to the base. Eric is noticeably better each time he goes out there. He's in control of the game. In his first couple starts, the game was moving really fast and he was exposed to some things. The blocking and the pitch receiving have grown so much and so fast to a very serviceable level right now. My messaging to Eric is he's gonna be a big-league catcher. When he's hitting, it's consistent bat to ball and his ability to impact it hard consistently. I look at Eric, I see a lot of Ben Rice. He's a guy who constantly gets his barrel to the ball. He hits for a high slug because he's able to consistently elevate the ball. He's still continuing to adjust and build his offensive profile. That's certainly not complete yet, which makes you even more excited about him because it is so good right now."

Age: 21 (22 on Sept. 10, 2026).

Manager Aaron Bossi's take: "Wilson is an extremely passionate player. I think of him as a glue guy. He speaks both languages, English and Spanish, and really brings the team together. He goes out wanting to win every single day. It's really awesome to see that in the minor leagues. I saw a lot of progress from Wilson this season. Manager Aaron Bossi's take: "If Jackson's not on our prospect list, I would absolutely be looking out for him because he's so sharp in middle of your infield and now he's showing the athleticism to do it in the outfield as well. title: Yankees Rivalry Roundup: Rays and Red Sox both take losses
description: The Yankees lost on Friday, but it didn’t cost them ground in the standings.
fullText:
The Yankees traveled north of the border on Friday, as they opened up a series against the Blue Jays. However, they left their bats — or whatever is left of them — back in the states. The lineup mustered just one run as they dropped the opener 3-1 to Toronto.

While the Yankees stunk up the joint yesterday, did anyone give them a helping hand in the various playoff races. Let's check in today's edition of the Rivalry Roundup.

The Rays very nearly climbed all the way out of a four-run hole in the ninth inning, but they fell one short, stranding the potential game-tying run at second as the Orioles finished things off behind Cam Sanders, snapping Tampa Bay's nine-game winning streak.

The two teams traded off runs in the second and third innings, with the O's taking 1-0 and 2-1 leads, only for the game to be tied by Tampa Bay shortly after. The game stayed tied for a while after that, as Chris Bassitt put in a solid effort for Baltimore fresh off the 60-day IL, matched by a combined effort by the Rays' bullpen.

The deadlock was broken when Dylan Beavers drove home two runs on a single in the seventh inning. Amid a deeply disappointing season, Gunnar Henderson then gave Baltimore some breathing room when he hit a two-run homer in the eighth. That seemed like it would be plenty enough, but it very nearly wasn't.

Tampa Bay started the bottom of the ninth with two singles and a wild pitch moving two runners into scoring position. Jonathan Aranda cashed in on that opportunity, driving home two runs with a single. A walk and a pair of stolen bases then put the tying run in scoring position, but Junior Caminero managed just a run-scoring ground out. Baltimore opted to issue an intentional walk Liam Hicks, which did put the winning run on base, but the gambit worked and the O's escaped and eked out the win. The Rays remain 6.5 games ahead of the Yankees and the O's got to within a game of the Tigers and Rangers for the last Wild Card spot — though the Twins and Blue Jays also sit between them.

Pittsburgh Pirates (60-64) 8, Boston Red Sox (65-57) 4: The Pirates got to Red Sox pitching to the tune of two home runs and eight runs in total, keeping Boston from gaining ground on the Yankees. Former Yankee prospect Rafael Flores Jr. got Pittsburgh on the board in the second, and the Bucs then scored a combined six runs over the fourth and fifth to fully take control of the game. In terms of pure numbers, the Red Sox actually recorded the same number of hits as Pittsburgh with nine, but the Pirates just did far more damage with their chances.

Chicago White Sox (63-58) 9, Detroit Tigers (60-62) 5: Miguel Vargas went 4-for-5 with two home runs and three RBI to lead the White Sox past the Tigers. Chicago took control of this game with a five-run fourth inning, which included a Munetaka Murakami homer and a two-run Braden Montgomery triple. The White Sox didn't have a particularly sterling pitching day, they just never remotely needed one; now, they're 3.5 games ahead of Detroit in the AL Central.

Houston Astros (63-60) 10, Seattle Mariners (57-66) 7 – 10 innings: An absolutely wild 10th inning saw the Astros give up two runs in the top of the frame before scoring five in the bottom of it to walk off with the win. Houston led for most of the game before the M's scored two in the eighth to tie things up and eventually send it to extras. Seattle then seemingly took control in the 10th, with a Victor Robles' triple leading the way to them putting up two runs. However, they couldn't hold that edge, and Christian Walker eventually sent everyone home with a three-run homer. fullText:
The New York Yankees lost their series opener against the Toronto Blue Jays, 3-1, on Friday night.

It was another inconsistent performance from Jazz Chisholm Jr., who recorded one hit in four at-bats and is now 5-for-his-last-35 at the plate.

One moment that stood out during the game came when Chisholm Jr. lost track of the number of outs in the inning.

With two outs, Chisholm Jr. watched the ball in the air after a Yankees hitter made contact. The Blue Jays eventually caught it to end the inning, but Chisholm Jr. reacted extremely late and nearly found himself in a costly situation.

This also isn't the first time this season that Chisholm Jr. has lost track of the outs while on the base paths.

— Dan Clark (@DanClarkSports) August 15, 2026

"Wow…how do they continue to put up with that," a fan said.

Someone else added, "Some players you watch daily and just respect. Some players you watch daily and lose respect. Jazz is a player you have to watch daily to really get it."

Another person wrote, "The only way you fix this is by pulling him from the game and benching his [explicit] for the weekend."

"He needs to be benched," a fan shared.

One more fan commented, "Tired of his act."

It's been a tough year for Chisholm Jr., and he'd be the first one to tell you that. He's discussed his struggles on several occasions this season.

"If I knew, I would already have fixed the problem," Chisholm said about his play. "Even when I think I'm getting going hitting, it's still an out. I'm still hitting it right at someone. I can hit it 107 (mph) and still hit it right at someone."

He's currently batting .216 across 394 at-bats with 85 hits, 17 home runs, 48 RBIs and 31 stolen bases.

title: Yankees' Carlos Rodon strikes out seven in potential final rehab start
description: Yankees left-hander Carlos Rodon followed up a strong first rehab start with a gem on Thursday night, pitching 4.1 scoreless innings and striking out seven batters for Double-A Somerset.
fullText:
Carlos Rodon followed up a strong first rehab start with a gem on Thursday night.

Pitching for Double-A Somerset, the Yankees southpaw tossed 4.1 shutout innings and allowed two hits and one walk while striking out seven batters.

After a delayed start due to inclement weather, Rodon took the mound and allowed a bloop single to lead off the game. Rodon bounced back, getting a fly out and an inning-ending double play to end the first frame.

Rodon then came out in the second, striking out two in a 1-2-3 inning. After Somerset put up a four-spot in the bottom half of the second, Rodon worked around a leadoff single by striking out the next three batters to keep New Hampshire off the board. Rodon struck out two more batters in the fourth before issuing his first walk to lead off the fifth inning. After picking up an out, Rodon was pulled in the middle of an at-bat after 58 pitches (41 strikes).

Tyler Boudreau came in to finish up the at-bat Rodon left for and got the third out without allowing Rodon's runner to score, putting an end to the veteran's night.

In his last rehab start, Rodon struck out four batters while allowing three runs on three hits and two walks across 2.2 innings. Thursday's start was a stark improvement as Rodon continues to build up his pitch count.

Earlier this week, Yankees manager Aaron Boone said this could be Rodon's final rehab start before rejoining the team. If Rodon feels good after Thursday's start, he can be activated next week, even with the limited pitch count. Boone actually stated that Rodon could continue to build up his count while pitching in a piggyback situation.

That could be a temporary solution for the upcoming rotation crunch that will befall the Yankees. When Rodon is ready to start games, New York will have to decide which of Will Warren or Ryan Weathers will be added to the bullpen.

title: Thanks to Yankees teammate, Jasson Dominguez made a change that could unleash Martian
description: A week after being demoted by the Yankees to Triple-A, Jasson Dominguez met up with NJ.com before a game this week in Allentown, Pennsylvania.
fullText:
ALLENTOWN, Pa. — Jasson Dominguez used to think that he was one of the hardest workers on his teams, and why not?

He always showed up on time. He always gave an honest effort. He never took shortcuts. He never got big-headed when the Yankees gave him a $5.1 million signing bonus at age 16 or when he was being compared to all-time greats before he played his first game as a professional.

Whether Dominguez was in the minors or was with the Yankees, he always cared about improving in all parts of his game, especially his fielding.

An American League scout who has watched Dominguez since he was playing Low-A ball in Tampa agreed.

"He never dogged it," the scout told NJ.com recently. "He worked hard. But he never was the hardest worker on his club. There was always someone next to him on the field giving more effort. It was noticeable that Dominguez wasn't going above and beyond to get better when others around him with half his talent were."

When that assessment was shared with Dominguez on Tuesday night before he played left field for the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre RailRiders, he responded with a smile and a nod.

"Oh, definitely," Dominguez said. "For sure. I've always worked hard, but definitely now I'm working more than what I used to do. That's from being in the big leagues and having great teammates."

Dominguez's work habits began changing late last season. When the Yankees upgraded their bench by trading for Amed Rosario, the hard-working journeyman infielder took Dominguez, a fellow Dominican, under his wing.

"Rosario is the guy that pushed me," Dominguez said. "He's a guy that literally came early every day to do his work and I started doing that with him."

When Rosario re-signed with the Yankees last winter, he pushed Dominguez during their spring training workouts on and off the field. Dominguez maintained a hard-working mentality when he started this season in the minors through his time with the Yankees, which also featured a stint on the injured list for a shoulder injury.

Rosario and Dominguez were separated again on Aug. 3, when the Yankees acquired outfielder Heliot Ramos at the trade deadline and rookie Spencer Jones was picked over Dominguez to remain in the majors.

Back with Scranton/Wilkes-Barre, Dominguez no longer needs anyone to motivate him.

"I felt pretty good with Rosario around and now I keep doing it because I understand that I've got things that I need to improve," Dominguez said. "I understand what needs to be done now. It's working harder than I ever worked, trying to get better and hopefully get back up to the big leagues."

Dominguez has been improving. In his first few years as a professional, Dominguez was so much better as a left-handed hitter that some scouts suggested that he give up batting right-handed. This year, he's been better as a right-handed hitter.

His outfield play is still below average, but his minus-1 Outs Above Average ranking in Baseball Savant's metrics is much better than last season's worst-in-the-league minus-9.

"I see a player who's constantly getting better, and that's the most important thing," RailRiders manager Shelley Duncan said. "Jasson has been in the spotlight a lot, and when you make mistakes with fundamentals or make mental errors in New York, it gets highlighted more than anywhere else in all of baseball.

"If you like take a guy like Jasson and that stuff happened in other places, it might slide under the radar and not even get noticed and you just chalk it up as a young guy learning. I say that because all of the mistakes that Jasson's made over his career, he learned from them and I've seen him grow as a player."

Dominguez will tell you that he's not close to his prime. He wants to live up to his Martian nickname and comparisons from his teenage years to Yankees legend Mickey Mantle and present-day superstar Mike Trout. That's a far-fetched dream, but he still has time to develop into an All-Star.

"I hope one day I can meet those reputations for sure, but at the end of the day, Mike Trout is Mike Trout and Mickey Mantle is Mickey Mantle," Dominguez said. "They've already done it. I'm trying to grow myself to be able to do it, too."

His opening act as a big leaguer featured a first-inning homer in his first game in Houston off future Hall of Famer Justin Verlander. He was 20 on Sept. 1, 2023. A few days later, he was headed for Tommy John surgery.

Almost three years later, he's been a mixed bag of highs, lows and more injuries. He's a career .243 hitter with 22 homers, 72 RBI, 36 steals and a .703 OPS in 741 plate appearances over 202 games.

In 2025, Dominguez batted .257 with 10 homers and 47 RBI in 123 games, but his fielding woes led to virtually no playing time in the final two months before he was sent back to Triple-A to open 2026.

He's crushed it in Triple-A this year, hitting .313 with six homers and 21 RBI in 33 games, but his numbers in 53 games with the Yankees were disappointing — .230 with six homers and 14 RBI in 53 games, most of them filling in right field for injured three-time MVP Aaron Judge.

"Jasson has what it takes to be really good," Scranton bench coach Gil Velazquez said. "He's disciplined. He's a good baseball player, period. He's still young and it takes a good amount of reps to be able to not get surprised with situations and not make dumb mistakes. Everybody goes through that."

Dominguez is still going through it. In his last full series, he misplayed a couple of balls in the right field corner at Wrigley Field. These were unforced mistakes in his mind, and they upset him.

"I want to improve the mental side," he said. "I have to make better decisions. That's one thing that I need to get better at."

That's part of the reason Dominguez is back in the minors.

After being optioned, he spent the allotted 72 hours he had to report to Triple-A at his New Jersey home with his family.

"I used those three days to reset my mind so I could go to Scranton with the best attitude," he said. "Obviously, I want to be in the big leagues, but it is what it is now. If I came down here with a bad attitude and pouted or whatever, that's not gonna help me get back up."

Dominguez trusts the Yankees are doing what's best for his career. He's focused.

"I want to improve my whole game," he said.

Slowly but surely, it's growing.

"He cut a ball down in the left-field corner and threw a runner out at second the other day," Duncan bragged. "His decision making and throwing is a lot better in the outfield this year. His focus pitch to pitch has gotten better every time I've seen him.

"It's fun watching Jasson hit because he's a carefree-loose type of hitter that can hit any type of pitcher. Those are fun hitters to have. He's got the talent and skillset to be a really good big leaguer for a long time."

title: Yankees At-Bat of the Week: George Lombard Jr. (8/8)
description: Lombard’s leadoff home run in the seventh inning against the Braves on Saturday turned out to be the game winner.
fullText:
I don't want to spill too much ink on the sorry state of the Yankees offense at the risk of sounding like a broken record. Instead, let's focus on the positives they have provided us in recent days, namely an improbable series win over the Braves. As much as the pitching largely carried the day, a certain young shortstop provided a handful of bright sparks on either side of the ball, and so George Lombard Jr. earns his first appearance on At-bat of the Week.

We join Lombard leading off the bottom of the seventh of the middle game against the Braves on Saturday. The Yankees are clinging to a 3-2 lead courtesy of a Spencer Jones RBI single in the second and RBI triple in the fifth, Austin Wells then driving him home with a double. Lombard enters this AB having struck out and drawn a walk against Chris Sale, the latter result requiring a pair of impressive, successful ABS challenges. However, Lombard now faces the hard-throwing righty reliever Victor Mederos, a very different look from the sidearming southpaw Sale.

Mederos starts Lombard with a first pitch sinker at 96 looking to tie the hitter up on the inner half.

This is a really good take from Lombard. The sinker looks like a strike on the upper ledge of the strike zone for much of its path toward home. It exits Mederos' hand aimed pretty centrally, yet Lombard is able to diagnose it immediately as a fastball and understands that the foot-and-a-half of arm side run will carry it all the way off the plate and out of the zone inside for a ball.

That was a pretty good pitch that Mederos just threw, so it makes sense that he sticks with the inside sinker as it's a pitch that can really eat up a hitter when buried in on the hands.

This is exactly why we don't bunt unless it is absolutely necessary. When you've got a reliever coming in and throwing upper-90s, a middle-middle sinker in a 1-0 count might be the best pitch you're gonna get to hit. Not only did Lombard miss a golden pitch to hit, but he lost his count leverage without making the pitcher work for it. Yes, I understand the third baseman was playing back and the Yankees are struggling for base runners at the moment, but Lombard was brought up to swing the bat (and for his glove) and bunting in this spot amounted to giving away a pitch.

Now that Mederos has shown Lombard a pair of fastballs that break toward him, he switches to a cutter breaking away from the batter, hoping he can get him to chase something off the plate outside should he mistakenly assume it is another sinker breaking in.

Mederos yanks this pitch way out of the zone, the pitch passing through the lefty batter's box and off the catcher's mitt to the backstop. It's one of the easier takes Lombard will get, though it was still informative for him to see a fastball that breaks in the opposite direction from the first two he saw.

After missing so wildly with that cutter, Mederos breaks out his third different fastball of the encounter, the four-seamer. His four-seamer breaks a little less down and a little less arm-side than his sinker, but the two pitch types otherwise aren't all that distinguishable from each other.

Mederos nails the outside edge with this 97 mph heater. He's partially able to catch Lombard looking by sequencing this pitch directly following a fastball that breaks glove-side, this pitch starting well off the plate away before tailing back into the zone, but mostly it's just a well-executed fastball that Lombard is more than justified to watch for a called strike.

Mederos now tries to leverage that called strike on the outside edge by sequencing a cutter that, as we mentioned, moves in the opposite lateral direction as his sinker and four-seamer. Lombard just watched a pitch that looked like a ball away end up as a called strike on the outside edge, so he effectively has to protect against anything that starts aimed away. This should make him susceptible to chasing a pitch that breaks glove-side.

Instead, Mederos grooves this cutter up and out over the plate. It doesn't have any of the cut of the first one he threw and flies straight as an arrow toward home. Lombard fires a beautiful swing lining this pitch into the seats in right for a leadoff home run to give the Yankees an invaluable late insurance run that they would need by the time the final out was recorded. I'll be honest, I did not realize Lombard had opposite field home run power, short porch or not. However, I love his approach, staying behind the baseball and allowing the velocity on the pitch to supply the power off the bat, knowing that with solid contact in the air, there's always a chance to leave the yard in right.

Without getting ahead of ourselves from a five-game sample, it is all the same assuring that Lombard has not looked overmatched facing big league pitching according to the eye test. We were always told that the defense was MLB-ready and indeed Lombard already looks way more rangy and self-assured at short than Anthony Volpe. However, I was not expecting him to have such an immediate impact with the bat. The power is certainly a welcome surprise, but it's his advanced pitch recognition and plate discipline that have really caught the eye and could be the keys to maintaining this form down the stretch.

title: New York Yankees vs. Seattle Mariners: Series Preview
description: The Yankees face a trident of right-handers as the scuffling Mariners dock in the Bronx.
fullText:
After three straight series against the Senior Circuit, the Yankees welcome the Mariners to the East Coast. The Bombers had an off day on Monday after dropping the series finale against the National League East-leading Atlanta Braves. The Yankees continue to hold serve as they wait for reinforcements to arrive, posting a 5-5 mark over their last 10 games, including an even 3-3 record thus far on the homestand.

The Mariners dock in New York after being swept at home by the pesky and, at this point, must-be-declared-legit Tampa Bay Rays. Seattle's season has not gone according to plan, as star catcher Cal Raleigh has struggled and the club enters play Tuesday sitting at 56-63. The Mariners have dropped four straight and are just 3-7 over their last 10 games.

This series features two night games before Thursday's getaway game, currently scheduled for 1:35 p.m. ET. Let's dive into which Mariners will be manning the harpoons and which Yankees white whales will be hoping to avoid the trident.

Tuesday: Ryan Weathers vs. Bryan Woo (7:05 pm ET)

Weathers has had a bit of an up-and-down first season in the Bronx. After opening the year looking solid, the month of June was not kind to the left-hander. However, since the calendar flipped to July, Weathers has found his footing again. Weathers currently has a 5-7 record, 3.79 ERA, and a 1.22 WHIP for the season.

Over his last three starts, he has thrown 18.2 innings while allowing just one earned run. That stretch includes six scoreless innings in his most recent outing against the Cardinals at home. Weathers has had his struggles in pinstripes this season, posting a 4.11 ERA at home compared to a 3.35 ERA on the road, but he will look to keep the ball in the yard and continue building on this recent momentum.

Woo is one of the best young pitchers in baseball, featuring a dominant four-seam fastball, excellent command, and the type of arm slot and tunneling that makes pitching nerds drool. The good news? Woo has been two very different pitchers this season.

At home, he owns an ace-like 7-0 record with a 1.96 ERA. On the road, however, Woo is 1-8 with a 6.71 ERA. That difference has held true recently as well. In his last two home starts, Woo has allowed just two earned runs across 13 innings. In his last two road starts, however, he has been roughed up for 10 earned runs in 10 innings. Those splits bring his overall season numbers to 8-8 with a 4.31 ERA and 1.12 WHIP. Expect Aaron Boone to send as many left-handed hitters to the plate as possible, as Woo's platoon splits also favor the lefties. Left-handed hitters have posted a .700 OPS against Woo this season compared to .585 from righties.

Wednesday: Will Warren vs. Bryce Miller (7:00 pm ET)

Much like Weathers, Warren has had his ups and downs throughout the 2026 season. Currently sitting at 8-6 with a 4.18 ERA, Warren's season has felt a bit like a roller coaster. After starting the year in dominant fashion, he has struggled as the weather has warmed. In July, Warren went 1-2 with a 5.47 ERA.

Warren has looked better in his last two starts. Against the Cubs, he tossed 6.2 scoreless innings, and in his most recent turn against the Cardinals, he allowed three runs over 5.1 innings. As one of the backend guys in this rotation, you have to expect some turbulence with Warren, take the good with the bad, and hope he can grind his way to a quality start.

The Mariners will send another power right-hander to the mound on Wednesday, as Miller gets the ball opposite Warren. On the season, Miller sits at 4-6 with a 3.08 ERA. He features an upper-90s fastball that he pairs with a nasty splitter and sweeper. Miller primarily uses the splitter to attack lefties and the sweeper against righties, and both pitches have been effective enough to produce almost identical platoon splits. Left-handed hitters have posted a .630 OPS against Miller compared to .629 from righties.

The good news for the Yankees is that, much like Woo, Miller has struggled away from the Pacific Northwest this season. At home, he owns a 2.09 ERA, while that number balloons to 4.02 on the road. More good news? The summer months have also been less kind to Miller, who currently finds himself in his worst stretch of the season. He has not made it through the sixth inning of a start since July 2nd.

Thursday: Max Fried vs. Logan Gilbert (1:35 pm ET)

The Yankees sandwich Warren with lefties as Fried takes the ball in the series finale. Fried has been steadily building himself back up after missing about two months of the season. Since returning, he has picked up right where he left off and currently owns a 4-3 record to go along with a tidy 2.88 ERA and 0.97 WHIP.

With two August starts under his belt, Fried looks ready for the postseason push. On the first of the month, he tossed 78 pitches of one-run ball against the Cubs before reaching 90 pitches while throwing 6.1 scoreless innings against his former club, the Braves, in his most recent start. I expect the training wheels to come off soon, and might I add that having a left-handed ace take the ball every fifth day is such an awesome thing to get to watch.

While the Yankees show a little spice of life on the mound, the Mariners roll out their third straight hard-throwing righty in Gilbert for the final game. Seattle's front office clearly has a type: tall right-handers who throw hard, get extension down the mound, and command all of their offerings. It is a good type, but with no real wrinkle from one day to the next, hopefully the Yankees' bats can lock in and light up Gilbert.

Gilbert owns an 8-7 record with a 3.42 ERA and 1.00 WHIP on the season. Unlike his other companions, Gilbert has actually been better on the road this year, posting a 2.50 ERA away from home compared to a 4.01 ERA at T-Mobile Park. In his most recent start against the Rays, Gilbert went 6.2 innings and took a tough 2-1 loss after allowing a pair of solo home runs that proved to be the difference. Tampa Bay also worked four walks, a season high for Gilbert.

The Yankees took two of three when they visited Seattle back in late March and early April. Here's hoping for more of the same this time around in the Bronx.

fullText:
NEW YORK — It sounds like Carlos Rodón will rejoin the Yankees' rotation soon.

The southpaw, out with elbow inflammation since June 30, is scheduled to make his first rehab start at Triple-A on Saturday. The plan is for Rodón to throw close to 50 pitches for the RailRiders.

From there, Rodón may or may not make one more rehab start, manager Aaron Boone said Friday. Either way, the Yankees will activate the pitcher before he's fully built up and "definitely probably piggyback him" in his initial starts, Boone said.

With a number of off days on the upcoming schedule and five healthy starters already in their rotation, the Yankees should be able to make that strategy work without taxing their bullpen. The long-held assumption has been that the Bombers will move Ryan Weathers or Will Warren to the pen anyway once Rodón returns, so either could be the piggyback pitcher while staying stretched out in this scenario.

Rodón, 33, went 4-2 with a 3.30 ERA over nine starts before going back on the IL.

He initially hoped to miss minimal time due to the inflammation, but he's been out over a month now. He said that multiple rounds of shots — he's gotten PRP and orthovisc injections — are to blame for the prolonged timeline.

"I always try to get back as quick as I can," Rodón said Friday. "I feel like anybody in this situation would. I wouldn't say anything delayed me. We just had a plan with the injections, and when you're scheduling injections and trying to throw in between them, it kind of makes it harder to figure out when you can throw, when you can't. Because when you get an injection, you might need a day off. Obviously, you take the first day off. You might need a couple more days.

So obviously, I would love to be pitching for our team right now. But right now, it's just building pitch count and getting in games, and that's it."

title: Nationals Announce Trade with Yankees, Additional Pitching Moves

fullText:
Roughly one hour after news broke, the second pre-deadline trade for the Washington Nationals was officially announced after sending Luis Garcia Jr. to the New York Yankees in exchange for four right handed pitchers: Jake Bird, Yovanny Cruz, Jack Cebert and Ben Grable.

While Cebert and Grable are in the second year of their professional careers after the Yankees selected both in last year's draft and are possibilities on the 2027 roster, Cruz and Bird arrive with MLB experience. Cruz touched 100 mph in his MLB debut, while also posting a 1.69 ERA and holding opponents to a .167 batting average across his first four MLB games. Bird, 30, arrives with plenty more experience having pitched in over 220 games after two seasons with the Yankees was followed by four seasons with the Colorado Rockies.

Bird allowed six earned runs across four games in his first season with the Yankees before then posting a 5.53 ERA and 1.54 WHIP across 36 appearances in 2026. The Nationals announced that Bird will begin his tenure with the organization in Triple A Rochester, but there are additional reinforcements on the way in the future.

Grable, rated the 19th-best prospect in the Yankees' farm system prior to the trade, was named a late replacement in the All Star Futures Game that Eli Willits and Miguel Sime also appeared in. Yet it's been his power that has been hard to ignore with his fastball touching 99 mph in 2026, adding young talent to potentially address the Nationals' biggest current weakness along the roster.

Yet it also came at a cost after the Nationals traded its longest tenured player in Luis García Jr. to the Yankees in exchange for the four right handed pitchers, giving president of baseball operations Paul Toboni the opportunity to sell high on the infielder who has enjoyed a breakout season under first-year manager Blake Butera.

While Andres Chaparro and Brady House will look to become to stopgaps at first base through the rest of the regular season, Garcia's presence will be a tough one to fill. CJ Abrams pointed to Garcia as the one who he first connected with the now star shortstop after first arriving in Washington DC via trade. Yet a potential divorce became growingly apparent through the month with growing noise about outside interest -- and the Nationals' willingness to listen.

Garcia noted the opportunity to head to the Yankees marks a "new chapter" in his career, but the chance to end his time in Washington in a season that has surpassed expectations marked the high note.

"A lot of great memories. A lot of great moments over my tenure here with the Nationals, and all I can say is that I love this organization. I love my teammates, the clubhouse, the coaches, staff, everyone."

While the Nationals are expected to announce additional roster moves ahead of Monday's series against the Philadelphia Phillies, Washington announced following the trade that Riley Cornelio will join Bird in Rochester, while PJ Poulin has also been transferred to the 60 day injured list.

title: Yankee’ Austin Wells pays in-game tribute on anniversary of Munson’s passing
description: Catcher Austin Wells pays tribute to late Yankees legend Thurman Munson by wearing vintage-style equipment on anniversary of his death
fullText:

The New York Yankees were able to come through with an important and well-pitched 2-1 victory over the Chicago Cubs Sunday at Wrigley Field. That gave the Yankees a series victory over the Cubs as they were victorious in 2 of 3 games.

Yankees catcher Austin Wells was behind the plate for the Yankees with ace pitcher Gerrit Cole on the mound. A look at Wells’ catcher’s equipment brought many raised eyebrows, because it did not have the modern appearance of so many at the position in the 2025 season. Instead, it was a throwback and an homage to Thurman Munson, the Yankees’ late and legendary catcher.

Munson was the captain of the Yankees and played a key role on the World Series championship teams of 1977 and ’78. However, he was tragically killed Aug. 2, 1979 when the small plane he was piloting crashed. While Munson has been gone for 47 years, his memory and his impact on the Yankees franchise remains strong. Wells’ paid tribute to Munson with the equipment that he wore against the Cubs.

Munson caught for the Yankees from 1969 through 1979. He was a seven-time All-Star in his career. He had a career batting average of .292 and he drove in 100 runs or more three times. While he is not in the Hall of Fame, many believe he deserves to be in the shrine.

More than the numbers, Munson is remembered for the fire he had behind the plate and his willingness to lead the Yankees into battle. He was always willing to block the plate and take the abuse of a runner crashing into him if it meant preventing a run from scoring.

He is remembered today as one of the team’s legends, and Wells was not about to let the anniversary of his death go without his tribute.

"Sometimes they've seen me dragging a little bit lately," he said in a post-match interview last month. "So they've been saying: 'Let's not forget who you are. You're the greatest in the world... you are Jazz Chisholm.'"

Chisholm exudes a self-confidence that has endeared him to Yankees fans well versed in big personalities and supportive of those who embrace their huge expectations.

Just this week he made headlines for a video in which he was asked to stay silent until he heard the name of a better player than himself.

He didn't say a word - even when the reporter mentioned team-mate Aaron Judge, who is widely regarded as one of the greatest Yankees ever.

But behind the sometimes brash front, there is a humble side to Chisholm.

Born in Nassau - the capital city of the Bahamas - Chisholm was raised mainly by his grandparents.

His maternal grandmother - Patricia Coakley - had been the star player of the nation's softball team. She began teaching her grandson how to hit a baseball from the age of two, and encouraged him to play with swagger and flair.

His paternal grandmother - Judy Chisholm - also played a vital role in keeping his baseball ambitions on track.

When Jazz was 12, he moved to Wichita in Kansas to attend boarding school - the best route to give himself a chance of becoming a professional athlete.

He soon became severely homesick and wanted to go home but Judy convinced him to tough it out.

After graduating and returning to the Bahamas, he was signed by the Arizona Diamondbacks through the international scouting process.

Bahamians are eligible to play for Great Britain in the World Baseball Classic - an international competition that is the closest thing the sport has to a World Cup.

Chisholm was part of the squad for this year's tournament in March - just weeks before the MLB season - and did not disappoint, captaining the team and batting in three runs in an 8-1 defeat of Brazil.

He has made no secret of his desire to represent Britain at the Olympics, but there are several hurdles to overcome.

First, the team have to qualify.

Only one European nation can book their spot in LA when qualifying takes place next year. The competition is open, but GB would probably have to go further than Italy, who unexpectedly beat the USA in reaching the semi-finals of the World Baseball Classic.

Then there are the eligibility criteria. Only athletes who are legally British citizens can compete for Team GB at the Olympics, so Chisholm would have to apply for a British passport.

The final sticking point is the Olympics fall right in the middle of the MLB season, so an agreement still needs to be reached to release players.

An 11-day mid-season break is the latest proposal that may suit all sides as the MLB aims to minimise disruption to its season and the International Olympic Committee looks to ensure it is able to showcase the game's best players.

"I think when you see an Olympic competition, you expect to see best on best," IOC sports director Pierre Ducrey told the BBC.

"That's what we delivered, for example, in ice hockey in Milan-Cortina with the return of the National Hockey League, and we hope we can see that materialising in LA.

"Baseball is a sport proposed by LA28, so they are leading those conversations but we, of course, support as much as we can with the hope that come 2028, we're going to see the best of the best going at it in the Dodgers Stadium."

Watch MLB Bases Covered Live: New York Yankees @ Chicago Cubs

For Chisholm, the Olympics can wait for now - because the immediate goal is to help the Yankees in their quest to secure a 28th World Series title.

The next step on that journey is a three-match series against the Chicago Cubs, with the final game live on the BBC from 19:10 BST on Sunday.

The Yankees haven't won the big prize since 2009, making this their longest run without the title since 1920.

They fell agonisingly short last season - losing to the Los Angeles Dodgers in the deciding game of the seven-game World Series - but are on course to reach the post-season again in 2026.

That gives Chisholm a route to living up to the tag he has been given to his team-mates - help the Yankees secure that long-awaited title.

title: Cody Bellinger injury adds urgency to Yankees trade deadline plans
description: Cody Bellinger's Grade 2 hamstring strain adds pressure on the Yankees to upgrade before the MLB trade deadline.
fullText:
Cody Bellinger’s worse-than-expected hamstring strain adds a new layer to the Yankees’ trade deadline period.

Diagnosed on Monday with a Grade 2 left hamstring strain, Bellinger’s four-to-six week timeline to return puts him back in the Yankees’ lineup sometime in September.

But even with Bellinger, a compromised Yankees lineup – no Aaron Judge since June 2, no Giancarlo Stanton since April 25 – had become a deeper issue.

Before their 9-5 win against the White Sox on Monday night, the second-place Yankees were 14-19 since June 19, averaging 3.27 runs per game.

Prior to that, the Yankees were averaging 5.27 runs per game and leading the AL East by 3.5 games.

Of course, every pinstriped hope of a deep October run is connected to Judge’s return.

And we’re still waiting on the second re-imaging of Judge’s fractured first right rib, and for his clearance just to begin baseball activity.

With Stanton, the constant he’s-getting-closer narrative should never limit the pursuit of more offense.

Still, impact bats are tough to find in this trade market, and you wonder about the appeal for the Yanks to absorb a bad contract or another DH-only type.

In recent days, potential offensive targets in Cincinnati’s Spencer Steer (wrist), San Francisco’s Casey Schmitt (knee) and even A’s catcher Shea Langeliers (knee), a longshot trade candidate, have receded due to injury.

A right-handed hitting outfielder is a better Yankee fit, and Kansas City has two impending free agents in Starling Marte and Lane Thomas. And the Mets' Tyrone Taylor is an increasingly intriguing option.

Elsewhere, if the Tigers choose to trade lefty ace Tarik Skubal, might they also be inclined to deal fellow impending free agent Gleyber Torres?

But the defensive fit in the Bronx is an issue, which also applies to Padres’ lefty-hitting second baseman Luis Arraez, also in his free agent walk year.

Still, the Bellinger situation doesn’t alter the Yanks’ top areas to upgrade.

The search for a swing-and-miss reliever and a right-handed hitting catcher could take the Yankees right up to Monday’s MLB trade deadline.

With an .856 OPS in nine games since his return from a left hamate bone fracture, right-handed hitting Minnesota catcher Ryan Jeffers – an impending free agent – is one possible target.

But the Twins are also three games back in the middling AL Central and one game behind for the last AL wild card spot entering Tuesday, so Jeffers’ trade status remains an interesting case.

And if there’s one huge trade to be made this deadline period, San Diego closer Mason Miller is the all-in candidate, with monumental end-game impact and team control through 2029.

If the Padres are inclined, lefty reliever Adrian Morejon – a free agent after this season – is a solid trade candidate. Plus, the Yanks’ past solid relationships with Luke Weaver and the rehabbing Clay Holmes (leg fracture) puts the Mets in play as a potential trade partner.

Bellinger’s absence further weakens the Yankees defensively, an overall area that needs to be addressed.

With appreciation of his utility value, Max Schuemann is an infielder playing out of position in left field, where Bellinger’s 19 defensive runs saved this year has boosted one of the league’s best pitching staffs.

For all his hard work and leadership, Amed Rosario is a liability at any defensive position, and he’s been less of a lefty masher this year, batting .197 overall in his last 25 games.

Top Yankees’ prospect George Lombard Jr. has initially struggled to hit each time he’s moved up a level, and you’d be asking a lot for him to debut in a pennant race.

But his plus-defensive skills at shortstop make him a prime candidate for an August call-up, as one more way to bolster the club’s pitching – its primary strength.

At last year’s deadline, the Yankees became a much better team down the stretch, in part, because of third baseman Ryan McMahon’s defensive presence.

Lombard could have that kind of impact even if he bats .208, which was McMahon’s average in 54 games after his arrival last summer from Colorado.

fullText:
The New York Yankees have been urged to move on from struggling third baseman Ryan McMahon, and the team could be getting an early glimpse of what it looks like without him in the lineup.

The team took McMahon out of the starting lineup for the first two games of their weekend set against the Philadelphia Phillies, the first time since April that he’s hit the bench for back-to-back games. The Yankees announced that veteran Amed Rosario would instead take third base and bat leadoff, leaving McMahon with an uncertain future as the trade deadline approaches.

The Yankees have not given further details on why McMahon has been sent to the bench against the Phillies, though he was healthy enough to come in as a defensive replacement for Rosario in the seventh inning of Friday’s 1-0 win over the Phillies.

McMahon also registered an at-bat in the top of the ninth inning, reaching first after being hit by pitch. He was solid in the field, recording a defensive assist in the eighth inning afte throwing out Alec Bohm.

But McMahon has struggled this season, leading to some speculation that the team could part ways with him before the upcoming MLB trade deadline. Reporter Devon Platana of SI.com suggested that the Yankees should “do whatever it takes to move on from McMahon and upgrade 3B, as he’s due to make another $16 million next season before becoming a free agent.” Platana noted that the Yankees would likely lose him for nothing in 2027, so the team should try to squeeze out whatever return they can manage this year.

While McMahon’s future with the Yankees could be murky, another infielder appears to be on his way out of the lineup. Shortstop prospect George Lombard Jr. is on the fast track to the Bronx this season, with reporter Jon Heyman noting that he should be with the team in a matter of weeks.

“Shortstop isn’t a top priority, partly due to faith in prospect George Lombard Jr., a terrific defender,” Heyman noted in the New York Post. “Recent estimates suggest Lombard could be up in about two weeks.”

That could mean the end of the line for Anthony Volpe, who like McMahon has struggled. SI.com reporter Joseph Randazzo noted that the team will likely keep shortstop Jose Caballero as a partner for Lombard, and could look to trade Volpe.

“While Caballero should still have a job on the Yankees as a roving infielder and outfielder, which is what he was for most of his career with the Tampa Bay Rays before coming to New York, it’s Volpe who should be the most concerned,” Randazzo wrote. “For one, Volpe only plays shortstop. Randazzo added that Volpe’s options with the team will grow more limited once Lombard arrives.

“Right now, the only options for Volpe are being traded or sent down to Triple-A,” Randazzo wrote. “If he wants to start, that would only happen if Lombard got hurt or they dealt him.”
